Iowa Continuing to Report Significant Damage and Disruptions Following Last Week’s Derecho Event Following a severe storm last Monday, communities across Iowa continue to report disruptions and damages. The storm, also known as a derecho, caused winds of almost 100 miles per hour, equivalent to a Category 2 hurricane. Cedar Rapids, the second biggest Iowa city by population, was one of the hardest-hit areas, in the central and eastern portions of the state. Eyewitness accounts in Cedar Rapids have described significant destruction with the majority of structures suffering damage and numerous local roads deemed impassable. An estimated 8,200 homes were damaged in the derecho across the state of Iowa. At least four deaths, three in Iowa and one in Indiana, have been blamed on the storm, which also caused widespread damage across the rest of the Midwest after moving east through Iowa. Upwards of two million people across the region lost power, including at least 600,000 in Iowa. 



In response to the storm, President Donald Trump approved a federal disaster declaration for Iowa that allowed for federal disaster aid for the state. In addition, Governor Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for 25 counties. The counties included: Audubon, Benton, Boone, Cass, Cedar, Clarke, Clinton, Dallas, Greene, Grundy, Guthrie, Hardin, Iowa, Jackson, Jasper, Johnson, Jones, Linn, Madison, Marshall, Muscatine, Polk, Poweshiek, Scott, Story, Tama, and Washington. In addition, the National Guard was deployed to Linn County to assist in recovery efforts there. Due to the extensive damage in the greater Cedar Rapids area, nightly curfews are currently in effect for Cedar Rapids, Belle Plain, and Tama. 



Assessment: While the majority of the Midwest has had power restored since last week, at least 65,000 people in Iowa, mainly in Linn County, remain without power as of this writing. Officials have warned some of the most hard-hit areas may remain without power for several more days due in part to the fact that thousands of miles of power lines were torn down and several thousand utility poles were damaged beyond repair. Linn County has also reported extensive telecom and internet outages in addition to the power outages. 



The storm has also caused widespread destruction to Iowa farmland, with an estimated several billion dollars in damages. Initial estimates from the U.S. Department of Agricultural (USDA) suggest at least 37.7 million acres of farmland were impacted across the Midwest, including at least 14 million in Iowa. The Iowa damage includes an estimated 8.18 million acres of corn and 5.64 million acres of soybeans, upwards of 43 percent of the state’s total crop. Farmers with affected crops have been advised to file loss claims immediately; however, officials have stated exceptions will be made to the rule requiring farmers to file such claims within 72 hours due to the ongoing power and telecom disruptions. Corn and soybeans represent a major part of Iowa’s economy, roughly $10 billion. Damage assessments remain ongoing and it remains to be seen whether any of the damaged crops are salvageable. While the damaged crops are a major part of the Iowa economy, it is not expected that crop loss significantly impacts the price and availability of those products for U.S. consumers. 



Derechos most often occur during the months of June, July, and August and typically impact the central and eastern regions of the United States; however, they are much rarer compared to regular or severe thunderstorms. To be classified as a derecho, a storm much produces winds of at least 57.5 miles per hour over a path at least 250 miles long and has no more than three hours separating individual wind reports. These types of storms move extremely quickly, often between 50 to 70 miles per hour, allowing them to cause damage over extensive portions of land. The storms often form with little to no warning and the Iowa derecho left residents with as little as 30 to 45 minutes to prepare for the storm. This was the second derecho of 2020 after the first traveled through Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and West Virginia at the beginning of June. That derecho also caused widespread damage, killing four people and leaving upwards of a million people without power. Due to the widescale damage these events can cause, the public is advised to always heed severe weather warnings from local authorities and seek shelter immediately. Those with interests in Iowa are advised to use caution due to the amount of storm debris remaining and continue monitoring developments related to the storm.

More broadly, the episode highlights how MMG Ltd mining operations at Las Bambas have repeatedly been interrupted by protests of late; the company has suggested that blockades of public roads have disrupted activities 95 days over the past year. Vietnam bans scrap import to keep its ports congestion-free Since May 2018, major ports in Vietnam such as Cat Lai Port and Hai Phong Port have faced severe congestions due to high volume imports of containers filled with paper, plastic and metal scrap materials. The congestion in Vietnamese ports may partially be the result of China’s ban on scrap imports since early 2018, prior to which, it used to allow half of the world’s plastic waste into the country. Due to the new environment policies adopted by China, many waste export businesses were left to find new emerging markets such as Southeast Asia to import their scrap materials. One country in particular is Vietnam, where waste import had increased since China’s ban. Sources indicate that the United States is the largest importer of scrap into Vietnam with around 147 million pounds of plastics imported between January and May 2018. This reflects an increase of about 85 million pounds from 2017 and 56 million pounds from 2016 respectively. 

In May, port operating companies and customs offices experienced capacity constraints with containers being left at ports for more than 30 to 90 days. In Cat Lai Port alone, there were about 8,050 TEUs of long-day stored goods, 5,234 TEUs of plastic and waste-paper materials and a remaining 2,816 TEUs of goods that were being stored for 90 days or longer. As a result, many imported goods were left in queue at Cai Mep and Tan Cang– Hiep Phuoc Ports before they were moved to Cat Lai Port, thus creating a ripple congestion effect at other ports. 

This led the authorities to impose a ban on waste imports on June 15. The ports also stopped accepting plastic scrap shipments effective at all ports from June 25 to October 15. The temporary ban not only buys time for the ports to clean up the abandoned containers but also provides an opportunity for the authorities to formulate short and long-term strategies to assess the ports’ storage capacity constraints and its plastic recycling industry. It is evident that for its short-term plan, legislative actions against unlawful imports of scrap would be taken as the port authorities reportedly started cracking down on illegal shipments of paper, plastic and metal scrap by investigating the owners of the containers and those responsible for the illegal imports. 

Furthermore, the port authorities will take the ownership of inspecting permits of imported scrap containers before allowing vessels to unload. Sources indicate that authorities also found companies that were deliberately importing illegal waste under a false name with fake licenses and incorrect addresses to earn quick profits while they leave their trash at the terminals. Hence, ports are now only allowing vessels to unload scrap containers if they have valid import permits and written date commitments to pick up the cargo.

Moreover, legal documents on the management of waste imports will be revised, taking into account environmental protections, and mechanisms to prevent, control & manage the trade and imports of scraps from other countries will be established. Despite these efforts, as of early October 2018, there were still reportedly 4,000 containers of scrap at Cat Lai Port which includes 3,000 containers that had been left for more than three months.

Although the scrap import ban is temporary and is expected to last only for a few months, it is likely that Vietnam will gradually reduce the import of overseas scraps and simultaneously increase the reuse of recycled materials in its long-term strategic approach. Solid waste ban had impacted local recycling industries, as sources suggested that waste processing is an additional source of raw materials for the country’s paper, plastic and steel industries. 

Despite the environmental and port congestion concerns, there is still a demand for overseas paper and plastic scraps for some domestic productions, due to the inadequate plastic recycling system in the country. Sourcing of scrap locally is reportedly difficult as most plastic wastes are normally mixed with regular trash and are not separated properly. Ho Chi Minh City alone produces about 900 tons of plastic waste daily, of which only 90 tons are recycled. While there are pros and cons in the scrap policy, efforts for local recyclers to switch to domestic waste will progress gradually in years to come as the industry needs time to adjust from handling import waste to domestic waste. 

It is not only Vietnam that needs to find a win-win solution for both ports and the domestic recycling industry; Thailand and Malaysia have also followed Vietnam’s footsteps in banning plastic waste due to an increase in such imports. On July 2, Thailand was the second country after Vietnam to ban the import of certain waste goods, including plastic scrap, electronic waste and hazardous waste at Ports of Laemchabang and Songkhla. However, unlike Vietnam, the duration of the ban remains unclear for Thailand. In the same vein, Malaysia has cancelled the import licenses for 114 of the country’s plastic scrap processors and implemented new operating procedures and regulations for recyclable material import licenses. Sources indicated that authorities will conduct inspections to ensure that only processors with valid permits are allow to continue operations. It is also important to note that Indonesia had begun inspecting 100 percent of scrap imports since early April following an increase in imports of scrap polystyrene from the United Kingdom in the first three months of this year. 

As most Southeast Asian nations take a tougher stance on waste import while they struggle with their own domestic waste problems, waste shippers are left with fewer options to find alternative markets to substitute China. It is no doubt that China’s ban has disrupted the global supply chain which had about 7 million tons of scrap plastic imported annually from the United States and Europe. Although India is likely to be the next location where waste exporters were reportedly shipping to, with volume up 164.4 percent to 70,550 TEU, there is no guarantee that this can remain a viable option in the long run. Perhaps, China’s import ban on scrap is a wake-up call not only for Southeast Asian nations but also for countries with large volumes of scrap to find solutions in its domestic market, particularly in the recycling sector.

Dispute around freight rates in Brazil lead to congestion at ports The nationwide trucker strikes that swept through Brazil during the last two weeks of May 2018 are continuing to have ripple effects throughout the country. The most recent developments in this regard have been the negotiations between the government and the truckers over minimum freight haulage rates known as the ‘tabela de frete’, or the minimum freight table. The most notable result of this persistent dispute is its effect on sea ports. 
Over the past several weeks, disputes between truckers and shippers have occurred at some of Brazil’s principal ports, such as Santos and Paranagua. This is evident in the backup of cargo at the aforementioned ports, triggered by a dispute between shippers and truckers on what the agreed freight prices are. Shippers claim that the post-strike rates are too high to make shipping affordable. Truckers, on the other hand, claim that the current rates were the best possible concession received during the course of the strike, and any contestation of the rates will lead them back to strike. 
A longer term issue lies with the government setting the definitive price schedule, which it has done so far through a provisional measure. This measure allows ANTT, a national ground transportation entity, to set the freight prices. The Brazilian Supreme Federal Tribunal, the highest court in the country, has heard the arguments posed by both the government and truckers in court on June 28, and is expected to announce its decision on August 27. 
This, however, does not alleviate the immense pressure that the industry will be under pending the decision. The continuing dispute has resulted in freight being stuck at ports, with cargo vessels and containers backed up and unable to move until freight rate disputes are resolved. No similar backlog has been reported in this context at any of the major international cargo airports in the country. The use of air freight as an alternative to circumvent the backlog at the seaports may be considered.
Agribusiness is the most immediately affected industry due to the perishability of the products involved. Until a decision is reached at the Supreme Federal Tribunal in August 2018, customers with cargo at Brazilian seaports are advised to keep abreast of new developments and, where appropriate, explore alternatives.

Wind Event to Impact Southern CA This Week; Dangerous Wildfire Conditions and PSPS Events Possible Meteorologists are predicting a new round of Santa Ana winds affecting Southern California this week. Winds are expected to gradually increase all week and winds of up to 65 miles per hour are possible by the end of the week in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. The high winds in combination with humidity in the single digits and no expected precipitation may create dangerous fire conditions. Though no warnings have been issued as of this writing, a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) event may be implemented at some point this week by Southern California Edison (SCE) to help mitigate the potential risk of a fire sparking due to SCE equipment. 



Assessment: Santa Ana wind events occur when strong winds blow from mountain ranges inland down towards the Southern California coast. These most often occur during the fall months but can extend into December. These wind events often spark some of the most destructive wildfires in Southern California especially when they occur at the same time as extremely dry conditions or above-average temperatures, as will be the case this week. A similar wind event occurred last week and resulted in a PSPS event that led to over 8,000 SCE customers temporarily losing power on Thanksgiving Day; however, no significant fires spread during that event. 



Though December is past peak wildfire season, California is still susceptible to destructive fires due to the wind events. In December 2017, the Thomas Fire burned over 281,000 acres in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties, making it at the time the largest fire in California history, and the rapid spread of the fire over an initial five-day period was blamed on a Santa Ana wind event. That fire destroyed over 1,000 structures and led to the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of residents. Additionally, the cause of the fire was found to be SCE equipment. Due to the potential for quick-spreading and potentially dangerous fires, businesses and residents in Southern California are advised to review and/or create emergency plans and evacuation routes. Cal Fire has created guidance on emergency wildfire plans that can be viewed at the following link: https://www.fire.ca.gov/media/4996/readysetgo_plan.pdf. Moreover, residents and businesses should prepare for potential prolonged power outages in the event of PSPS events implemented by SCE. Details on any potential events can be viewed at the following site: https://www.sce.com/wildfire/psps. Heed all instructions from local authorities.

Ecuador   No major protest activity reported after an agreement was reached. Incident closed. There have been no indications of major protest activity, and protesters have lifted most road blocks across Ecuador. An agreement was reached between government officials and protest groups on October 13, which included the government withdrawing orders to terminate fuel subsidies and protest groups agreeing to end protests. Celebrations occurred in the streets of Quito overnight following the announcement. Dozens of highways were shut down by roadblocks and/or large groups of protesters across 17 different provinces during the actions; however, most of these have since been lifted. As a result, intercity travel and cargo transportation has resumed, including fuel transport which was disrupted. Furthermore, a curfew in areas of Quito has been lifted. 

There were sporadic reports of looting and vandalism across the country during the unrest. Mobs of protesters broke into multiple government offices throughout Quito, and President Lenin Moreno temporarily relocated the government to the city of Guayaquil. At one point, protesters occupied the House of Culture in Quito and took eight police officers and 27 journalists hostage. Outside of the capital, protesters seized and/or vandalized multiple oil fields, in some cases causing production stoppages. Ecuador s ministry of energy reported that oil production fell by roughly 31 percent; however, production has resumed and is expected to return to normal. Public demonstrations repeatedly degenerated into violent clashes with security forces. Tear gas and water cannons were used to disperse large crowds. Police vehicles and at least one armored personnel carrier were set on fire and destroyed. During the unrest, at least eight people died, 1,340 were injured, and 1,192 were detained. Ecuador's Red Cross suspended paramedic and ambulance services due to security concerns. The recent bout of unrest was sparked when the government passed a bill terminating fuel subsidies. This incident is closed.

Port of Cape Town issues new instructions over coronavirus outbreak Media sources reported that the harbor master at Cape Town has issued instructions due to the coronavirus outbreak:
•	Prior to boarding a vessel, Port Control should be contacted to confirm Free Pratique has been received and enquire about the last three ports of call. Security to also check with ISPS pre-arrival notification.
•	Upon boarding, Health Status of crew to be conformed with the Master.
•	For high risk vessels (those that have been to China, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, United States potts), boarding officers to wear face mask and gloves.
•	For the warning period, all South African citizens should refrain from consuming foods or liquids on board vessels from high risk areas. Gifts of food should not be accepted.
•	All off port limit crew from affected areas to be carefully screened – no crew to be taken off vessel without Port Health clearance.
•	Port Health declaration also required for all Off Port Limit transfers.
•	Medical evacuations from vessels from affected areas to be screened by Port Health before the person is taken off the vessel.
•	Captain to confirm in writing stowaway sweep was conducted before departing last port. Stowaway search may be requested when alongside, at the vessel’s cost, using specialist companies whose staff have undergone Corona Virus Disease training and/or awareness.
•	Security to inform Port Control of any reported stowaways from vessels calling from affected areas. If reported, vessel must remain at anchor until cleared by Port Health for entry or advised otherwise.
•	Masters must report stowaways on board if vessel calling from an affected area. Vessel to remain at anchor until stowaways are examined and cleared by Port Health or otherwise advised.
•	Strict gangway watches to be maintained at all times.
•	All involved in evacuation of infected crew or stowaways must be trained by Port Health on Corona Virus.
•	Separate lists of vessels calling from Corona-affected areas to be maintained for record purposes.
•	All galley waste of vessels from affected areas to be incinerated and should not be accepted ashore.
•	Additional security to be deployed by the agent for contaminated vessels and no-one to be allowed on board a contaminated vessel except Port Health. Only after clearance can anyone be permitted to enter the vessel.
•	If possible, contaminated vessels should be allocated an isolated berth away from other vessels.
Importers are advised to follow the recommended measures to avoid shipment delays as well as to prevent the virus.

Arrests of Protest Leaders and Banning of Demonstrations Likely to Worsen Hong Kong Situation On Friday, police arrested a number of prominent figures in the pro-democracy movement, including members of the Demosisto party Joshua Wong Chi-fung and Agnes Chow Ting, and pro-democracy lawmakers Cheng Chung-tai, Au Nok-hin, and Jeremy Tam Man-ho. In total, at least 28 people were arrested. Their charges were related to protests that have taken place in recent months. Joshua Wong and Agnes Chow have since been released on bail, given evening curfews, and have been prohibited from entering the Admiralty area.

The day before, police also prohibited the main rally called by the Civil Human Rights Front (CHRF) on Saturday, citing the risk of violence due the history of other protests. Police said that they received credible intelligence that some protesters were planning to use petrol bombs, tasers, and drones against police. The protest was scheduled to start at Chater Garden in Central and end at Beijing s Hong Kong Liaison Office in Sai Wan. An appeal filed by the CHRF was denied and as a result, the march was officially canceled. However, a number of protesters have said that they intend to defy the ban and hold the protest march anyway. Police also banned a protest scheduled to take place on Monday at Salisbury Garden in Tsim Sha Tsui in Kowloon that was meant to coincide with a two-day strike called by the Confederation of Trade Unions and other groups.

Reports also emerged that earlier in the summer, the Hong Kong government was prepared to make a key concession to the protesters in officially withdrawing the extradition bill that sparked the recent rounds of protests. However, Beijing rejected the plan and instructed Chief Executive Carrie Lam to not withdraw the bill, open a police inquiry, or make any concessions to the protesters. The plan was reportedly submitted to the Central Co-ordination Group for Hong Kong and Macau Affairs and was reviewed by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Assessment: The arrest of the prominent pro-democracy figures, the banning of protests, and the refusal to make any concessions are likely to worsen the situation in Hong Kong in the immediate future. These actions will likely further radicalize a portion of the more moderate protesters and some of the already more violent protesters now have even less reason to temper their actions if they feel that there are no other options. The mass arrests were also likely timed to take place ahead of the five-year anniversary of the release of the plan for limited democracy for Hong Kong on August 31, 2014. Dissatisfaction over the plan, which required all candidates for chief executive to be approved by a pro-Beijing committee, sparked the Occupy Central protests later that year.

South Africa’s road freight in jeopardy amid xenophobic attacks on foreign drivers Cargo trucks driven by foreign nationals in South Africa have faced violent attacks by local truck drivers and other unknown groups since the beginning of the year and the situation has worsened in recent months. The recent attacks escalated after truck drivers affiliated with the National Truck Drivers Founders and All Truck Drivers Foundation (ATDF) issued an ultimatum for foreign truck drivers to vacate their jobs by December 1. This is because South Africans associated with the foundation believe that truck driving is not a specialized skill and can be done by a local driver. Protests against foreign truck drivers have been well-attended in urban centers, and interstate highways and key thoroughfares have been blocked intermittently. 

The anti-foreign sentiment towards foreign truck drivers and their employers in South Africa is not uncommon and the recent unrests associated with the hiring of foreign truck drivers in South Africa are expected to persist over the coming weeks, as the South African National Cargo Transport Drivers Association on December 17 has given 21 days to the National Bargaining Council to deregister all foreign truck drivers. The situation remains fluid, as foreign truck drivers have also threatened to ban South African drivers from entering neighboring countries if they are forced out of their jobs. 

Targeted highways:
Although South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa has condemned the xenophobic attacks, little has been done to protect road freight logistics. Since November 19, 35 cargo trucks have been petrol-bombed. According to media sources, 9 trucks were set alight on the N3 highway during the course of a day, before the foreign drivers were attacked and their cargo looted. Other attacks include vandalism and road blockades with burning tires, making it impassable for vehicles. On November 23, a driver was fatally shot and another injured. The following roads and locations have been targeted since late November: 

•	Kwa Zulu-Natal province: N3, R103, R23, and R550 roads 
•	Free State province: the R59 between Parys and Sasolburg 
•	Gauteng province: N3 in Johannesburg, N12 in Benoni, and R21 in Boksburg 
•	Mpumalanga province: Key routes in Bethal 

In retaliation, foreign truck drivers have threatened to block South African truck drivers from crossing land borders into other neighboring countries, if they are forced to leave their jobs in South Africa. Any such attempts may lead to unrest at cross-border points resulting in congestion or delays for freight trucks and customs processing time, which is already significantly impeded by COVID-19 restrictions. 

Impact on road freight:
South Africa relies heavily on the road freight sector as about 90 percent of freight moves via land transport, particularly the N3 highway that connects between Johannesburg and Durban. It is also used as a key route to transport export and import goods from the Port of Durban to the capital. In recent months, the industry has been hampered by varying disturbances, including traffic congestion at border points, increasing cargo thefts, protests, and violence related to socio-economic issues resulting in road blockades, and mounting storage and demurrage costs on imports and slower freight clearance. In September, cargo trucks faced congestions at South Africa’s border checkpoints with Mozambique, Botswana, and Zambia as protesters against foreign truck drivers and blocked roads. 

Additionally, the South African economy is still reeling from the effects of the COVID-19 lockdowns. When the government imposed a level-5 COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020, local importers had to bear the storage and demurrage cost of around ZAR 1.4 billion (USD 95 million; EUR 77 million) while over 20,000 containers were left in storage facilities, according to the South African Association of Freight Forwarders. While the economy is still at a recovery stage, the recent protests against the hiring of and attacks on foreign truck drivers have caused panic amongst some logistics companies in utilizing their assets and resources, with some haulers having to downsize jobs as trucks stand idle. 

Anti-foreign sentiments:
Demonstrations and attacks against foreign truck drivers are not uncommon in South Africa as there is a widely held perception that trucking companies favor hiring foreign nationals as they accept lower wages. Moreover, the conflict comes at a time of high levels of unemployment amid the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic, fueling xenophobic sentiments across the country. According to the South African Labor Ministry, at least 84 attacks have been registered since April 2020 over the employment of foreign truck drivers. While the ATDF claims that its motive does not stem from xenophobia, precedents indicate that the same type of aggression was directed specifically at foreign drivers and their employers.  

Resiliene360 customers with business in South Africa are advised to monitor local developments by liaising with local representatives or suppliers to stay abreast of potential escalations in order to coordinate changes to delivery schedules. Arrests, Clashes with Authorities Following Sentencing of Quim Torra; Further Protests Likely On Monday, September 28, the Supreme Court officially supported the decision of the Superior Court of Justice of Catalonia (TSJCAT) to sentence Catalonian President Quim Torra for a crime of disobedience and effectively remove him from office. The initial ruling of TSJCAT banned Torra from government office for a period of 18 months and fined him EUR 30,000 for refusing to take down a banner supporting pro-independence leaders from the balcony of the regional government’s headquarters in March 2019. The banner reportedly referred to former Catalan cabinet members, legislators, and activists who had been imprisoned or left the country following a 2017 declaration of independence. Torra’s deputy, Pere Aragones, is expected to take over as president-in-charge until the regional parliament elects a new leader or a new election is held. Pro-independence activists have called for protests across Catalonia, with several demonstrations taking place across the province of Barcelona on Monday. Protesters allegedly threw pigs’ heads, building materials, stones, and a firecracker at Mossos d’Esquadra guarding the Public Prosecutor’s Office. A march was held in Jardinets de Gracia, thousands attended a socially distanced rally near Placa de Tetuan, and approximately 60 people demonstrated in front of the Palafolls City Council. Protesters who gathered at Ciutadella Park reportedly broke into one of the entrances granting access to the Parliament’s doors and were dispersed by Mossos d’Esquadra, following which some of them continued to protest at Ronda de Sant Pere, where they reportedly set up barricades and burned containers. The demonstrations were called by organizations such as the Committees of Defense of the Republic, Omnium Cultural, and the Catalan National Assembly. At least five public disorder arrests were made during the demonstrations.



Assessment: While there has been opposition to TSJCAT’s decision, including a manifesto denouncing the disqualification of the president published by the Catalan National Assembly of Andorra, the Supreme Court judged that the decision did not violate Torra’s right to free speech, just limited what he could do in his role as an elected official. Torra’s predecessor, Carles Puigdemont, was removed from office following the 2017 push for the region’s independence, fled to Belgium, and had fought extradition to Spain. Nonetheless, Torra has stated that he will take his appeal against the ruling to European courts, purportedly including the Strasbourg Court. He has also called on Catalans to turn the next elections, scheduled for February 7, 2021, into a “de-facto plebiscite on independence” by voting for separatists. Polls and election results, however, suggest that there is a more or less even split among the 7.5 million Catalan residents on the subject of independence from Spain. Further demonstrations are expected in the run-up to elections. It is advised to continue to monitor developments in the time leading to the elections due to ongoing tensions over Catalan independence from Spain. It is also advised to avoid all protest activity due to the likelihood of arrests and the potential for clashes between pro- and anti-independence demonstrators, as well as with authorities.

It also removes some tax and environmental regulations for companies. The Confederation of Indonesia Trade Unions and other associations have embarked on a general strike through Thursday in opposition to the bill, with as many as five million people expected to participate. The bill drew largescale protests on multiple occasions in the months before its passage, and demonstrators gathered in various cities across the country on Monday and Tuesday.



Assessment: While the authorities have not explicitly said that protests related to the job law are banned, police officials have stated that large gatherings will remain barred under COVID-19 gathering restrictions. Tropical Storm Beta Forms in the Gulf of Mexico Bringing Flooding Threat to the Texas Coast Tropical Storm Beta formed in the Gulf of Mexico on Friday and is currently located approximately 360 miles southeast of Corpus Christi, TX. The storm is forecast to meander through the gulf before making a westward turn on Sunday and strengthen into a Category 1 hurricane. Landfall for the storm remains uncertain; however, Beta is expected to move up the Texas coast and could potentially make landfall south of Houston on Tuesday or Wednesday. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) has not issued watches or warnings related to the storm as of Friday afternoon; however, the NHC warned these are likely beginning Friday night or on Saturday. The most up-to-date details on the storm, including path and strength, can be found at the following link: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/. 



Assessment: Significant uncertainty exists regarding the current path and eventual strength of Beta. Initial estimates suggest that Texas communities along the coast from Brownsville to Houston could see upwards of 12 inches of rain from the storm. Officials have cautioned that the slow-moving nature of Beta could lead to a scenario that just occurred with Hurricane Sally in Florida and Alabama. Sally’s slow movement prior to and during landfall allowed for excessive rainfall with some areas, such as Pensacola, FL, reporting over 25 inches of rain and life-threatening flooding. Though none have been issued as of this writing, evacuations remain a possibility for coastal communities in Texas as the path and strength of the storm become clearer. Due to the potential impacts and uncertainty, those with interests along the Texas coast are advised to closely monitor developments related to Tropical Storm Beta. Emergency plans, potential evacuation routes, and disaster supply kits should be prepared and reviewed.

U.S. Mission Issues Alert as Protests Escalate and Militants Threaten Attacks on Oil Facilities On Tuesday, the U.S. Mission in Nigeria issued the following Protest Alert for U.S. citizens in the country:



“Multiple demonstrations are ongoing across Nigeria – to include areas within the consular districts of Abuja and Lagos.  Although most demonstrations are peaceful, some have become violent and have shut down major thoroughfares and bridges.  Some police stations have been targeted.  Lagos State closed all schools indefinitely as of October 19 due to protests and implemented a 24-hour curfew starting at 4:00 p.m. on October 20.  Consulate General Lagos is closed for the rest of today and tomorrow. 



We continue to urge all U.S. citizens to avoid areas around protests and demonstrations and to check local media for updates and traffic advisories.  Continue to be vigilant and avoid areas affected by the protests.”



The entire Protest Alert can be viewed at the following link: https://ng.usembassy.gov/health-alert-u-s-mission-nigeria-37/



Assessment: Protests over alleged police brutality have escalated across Nigeria over the last few days, as demonstrators have attacked and torched a number of police stations, including in Lagos and Oyo, and helped orchestrate a prison break in Edo state over the weekend. Security forces and unidentified thugs have also continued to attack and clash with demonstrators, leaving at least 18 people dead since the protests began on October 8, including four on Monday alone. In response to the escalating violence, police have announced plans to deploy anti-riot police nationwide; however, the move could further exacerbate tensions and heighten the risk of further clashes between the two sides.



Additionally, there have been reports that militants in the oil-rich Niger Delta region have expressed solidarity with the demonstrators and threatened renewed violence if the demonstrators’ demands are not met. The Reformed Niger Delta Avengers (RNDA) issued a statement that its fighters have been placed on standby to engage Nigerian troops and resume attacks on oil facilities. In particular, the RNDA has singled out the Escravos-Warri-Kaduna distribution pipeline, Chevron Valve platform, Shell Forcados Terminal, Escravos trans Lagos pipeline, Escravos Tank Farm, and the Bonny Export Terminal. The threats suggest that militant groups could be exploiting the protest movement, broadening the demonstrators’ demands, and could heighten the risk to critical infrastructure, such as oil facilities.

IRGC Fires Missiles at Mock US Aircraft Carrier in Show of Force Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) launched underground ballistic missiles at a replica US aircraft carrier during military exercises in the Strait of Hormuz, near the port city of Bandar Abbas, on July 29. As a result, US troops were reportedly put on alert at the al Dhafra Air Base in Abu Dhabi and the al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. One day prior, the IRGC fired a missile from a helicopter targeting the same fake carrier. Wednesday was expected to be the final day of the maneuvers, in which several units from IRGC’s Navy and Aerospace Division took part. Such military exercises have the potential to result in casualties in cases of mistaken fire, though the maneuvers on July 28 and 29 passed without incident.



Assessment: The incident appears to be geared toward demonstrating Iran’s strength of its missile program, and intimidating US troops in the area. While, an Iranian military commander stated that this was Iran’s first successful attempt to carry out the launch of underground ballistic missiles, the military is known to have vast underground bases hiding its ballistic missile arsenal. In addition to highlighting the country’s network of subterranean projectiles, the military exercises also underline the lingering threat of military conflict between Iran and the US, after a series of escalating incidents last year led to a drone strike in January 2020 that killed Qassem Soleimani, the commander of the IRGC’s Quds Force. Additional incidents, including US officials calling for the UN weapons embargo on Iran, set to expire in October, to be renewed, and an incident on July 23, in which US fighter jets reportedly flew too close to an Iranian passenger plane near Beirut, have also renewed tensions. Despite appearing to heighten tensions, the maneuvers are likely only a show of force designed to intimidate the US, and do not necessarily increase any likelihood of direct confrontation between the rivals.

Likely collapse of Yemen's Hodeidah ceasefire and government offensive... Risks: Civil war, TerrorismSectors or assets affected: Marine, Ground cargoThe Houthi movement announced at a news conference in Sanaa on 16 March that its forces would strike Riyadh and Abu Dhabi with ballistic missiles if the implementation of the United Nations (UN)-sponsored peace deal in the port city of Hodeidah was breached. The Houthis claimed to have intelligence that the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and the UAE, is preparing to resume its offensive on the port city. The Hodeidah ceasefire came into force on 18 December 2018, but there has since been no progress on implementation of a joint withdrawal from the city. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are reportedly now insisting that they are no longer willing to wait.Significance: IHS Markit assesses that the fundamental disagreement between the Houthis and the government over who will provide the 'local forces' to provide security in Hodeidah after a withdrawal is unlikely to be resolved peacefully, and that the UN-sponsored ceasefire is very likely to collapse in the coming weeks. Should this be the case and a government offensive to recapture the city goes ahead, there would be a severe risk of indiscriminate property damage in the city and the adjacent port from Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and shelling, and protracted urban warfare. Faced with the loss of Hodeidah, the Houthi movement would most likely destroy port facilities and deploy sea mines, making the port unusable for at least several months, and resume missile and IED attacks against coalition shipping in the Red Sea. An indicator signalling an imminent government offensive would be an intensification in shelling of Hodeidah's southeastern neighbourhoods. An agreement by both sides to further face-to-face talks on a specific date would at least temporarily reduce the likelihood of a government offensive. In the event of a government offensive, Houthi retaliation would probably also involve the launch of 'Scud'-type missiles and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) strikes at military and infrastructure targets against Saudi Arabia, although their impact would be mitigated by Saudi Patriot air defences. Houthi UAVs are unlikely to have the range to strike targets in the UAE, despite a claimed UAV attack.                     Content provided by IHS Markit Foresight © 2019

Protests and Clashes in Hong Kong around the New Year a Sign That Unrest Is Likely to Continue On Wednesday, protesters gathered for an approved march from Victoria Park in Causeway Bay to Chater Garden in Central. Organizers claimed that over one million people participated in the march, while police said that attendance was around 60,000. Violence took place just a few hours after the march started, with some protesters vandalizing a HSBC branch in Wan Chai. Police responded to the scene and clashed with protesters, using pepper spray and tear gas to disperse those in the area. A Starbucks store was also vandalized in Tin Hau. The march was ordered to end at around 5:30 PM but thousands refused to return home, and later blocked roads, vandalized buildings, and threw objects in multiple areas, including Wan Chai, Central, and Causeway Bay. Police used tear gas, water cannons, and pepper spray. Around 400 people were arrested, with the majority detained in a single police operation near SOGO in Causeway Bay.

Assessment: The large turnout on New Year s Day and the violent clashes that followed shortly after is a clear sign that unrest is likely to continue for at least the near future. The level of violence is still lower than what was seen in October and early November, where protesters held multiple days of disruptive actions, first in early October with the National Day protests and the face mask ban, and then in November with the citywide strike and takeover of universities. There was a brief lull in demonstrations in the immediate lead up and aftermath of the local district council elections in late November, but protest activity began to increase again in December, with shopping centers targeted and central and southern Kowloon (Tsim Sha Tsui, Yau Ma Tei, and Mong Kok), along with northern Hong Kong Island, seeing disruptive demonstrations and violent clashes. Overall, the protests since December have been more geographically contained when compared to those in October and early November, making the disruptions easier to predict and less widespread, although this may not hold true in the future, as the movement has shown that it is adaptable and can change tactics quickly. Customers should continue to exercise a heightened level of caution at all times, as protests may be called with little notice in advance, and all demonstration activity should be avoided due to the risk of clashes.

Container terminals close gates in Genoa following bridge collapse; to reopen on August 16 Transportation and logistics in and around the port city of Genoa have been paralyzed since midday on August 14 after the central span of the Morandi Bridge, a flyover bridge supporting the A10 highway, collapsed onto rail tracks and warehouses. Container terminals at the Port of Genoa, located about 5 kilometers from the bridge, have preemptively closed their gates on August 14, preventing trucks from entering the gates to load or unload containers. Vessel operations were said to continue as usual, and gates are expected to reopen by August 16. 

Road and rail traffic throughout the city of Genoa has already been significantly compromised since August 14. With only one bypass available via the SS1 road and bridge construction works likely taking months before completion, congestion, delays and additional fees will likely affect road, rail and ocean freight transportation from and to Genoa over the coming months. Customers should be mindful of the following transportation impacts when planning shipments to, from or through the Genoa area: 

1.	Cross-terminal movements between the major container terminals VTE and SECH in Genoa, which are linked by the Morandi Bridge, are likely to suffer delays. This is expected to affect export containers in transit, which may miss cut-off times on vessel services. 

2.	Container movements between Genoa and industrial centers such as Torino and Milan in Italy, as well as the French border near Menton, is likely  to experience extended delays as trucks are re-routed via smaller, congested connection roads towards the A12 highway to the north or the A10 highway to the west. 

3.	As rail tracks are likely to remain closed in the short term, potential alternative modes of transportation such as intermodal rail traffic from the Port of Genoa to Milan will also be affected by the bridge collapse. Since containers from Milan are usually connected to Germany through the important Rhine Alpes Rail Corridor via Switzerland, rail exports from factories located in the port area of Genoa are expected to face delays and congestions. Factories in the area include the Ilva steel mill that supplies hot-rolled steel to automotive, packaging and energy customers. 

Customers are advised to monitor recovery efforts in the area and consider the aforementioned impacts to transportation when planning cargo movement in the area.

Stalled contract negotiations may result in strike or lockout at Port of Montreal Shipping sources reported this week that dockworkers at the Port of Montreal, Canada, are considering going on strike as talks between port employers and the union have stalled and a labor contract agreement has expired since December 31, 2018. Risks: Labour strikes; Protests and riotsSectors or assets affected: Marine; Cargo; Property; AgricultureOn 19 December, Valparaiso port contractor workers rejected a preliminary agreement mediated by the government to call off a 34-day strike over working conditions and bonuses. The agreement offered them soft loans and other benefits totalling CLP1.37 million (USD1,980), lower than the CLP2 million bonus workers demanded. Confrontations between demonstrators and the police at the port neighbourhood, Colon Avenue, and the city centre, involved protesters erecting barricades using burning tyres, and throwing sticks, stones, and Molotov cocktails at the police, who responded using tear gas and water cannons. Some demonstrators broke windows of nearby property and stores, and looted the offices of maritime company Ultraport. At the union headquarters, approximately 25 individuals threw blunt objects and Molotov cocktails from the roof, which led to the police breaking into the premises and arresting 16 people. Valparaiso's union is calling workers at other ports to join the strike. According to the company Empresa Portuaria de Valparaiso (EPV), over USD4.9 million in losses have been incurred as a result of this dispute.Significance: There is a high risk of nationwide strike action Chilean ports, with unions at other ports joining in. Port workers at 10 other terminals throughout the country (Bio Bio, Caldera, Coronel, Iquique, Lirquen, Penco, San Antonio, San Vicente, Talcahuano, and Ventanas) have already carried out partial stoppages in solidarity, mainly during the night shifts, indicating growing likelihood of escalation. Broadening strike action at Chile's ports would cause severe export disruptions and delays to maritime cargo. In 2013â14, three-weeks' long strikes across Chilean ports caused losses totalling approximately USD300 million. The agriculture sector would be particularly affected, as this is the middle of their export season. Fruit exports in December have already declined by 95% compared to the same period in 2017, according to media reports. Should the government present a bill improving compensation and working conditions for contractor workers, this would indicate improved likelihood of resolution and declining labour strike risk at Chilean ports. Upper Texas Coast   Recovery efforts are underway in the region; impacts remain. Incident closed. While flood waters continue to recede across the eastern coast of Texas, relief and recovery efforts are underway in the region. As a result of flooding caused by the passing of storm Imelda, a total of five people were killed. On Friday, September 20, two bodies were discovered in the Beaumont area, and one was discovered in Houston. There are reports that flood waters have begun to recede in the area, and although rain is in the forecast for the weekend September 28, favorable weather is also predicted. Officials are continuing to survey flooded areas with regard to search and rescue efforts. Governor Greg Abbott declared a state of disaster in 13 counties in response to the severe flooding. The proclamation was for the following counties: Brazoria, Chambers, Galveston, Hardin, Harris, Jasper, Jefferson, Liberty, Matagorda, Montgomery, Newton, Orange, and San Jacinto. There are no immediate reports regarding the current status for each individual county.

The most substantial flooding was reported in Chambers County, specifically in Winnie. In Harris County, the most significant was in Houston, and in Jefferson County, the largest reported flooding was in Beaumont. As of September 25, the only counties under active flood warnings are Jasper, Jefferson and Hardin. Evacuations were issued for residents in Hardin and Jefferson counties. Several other counties were under shelter-in-place orders during the storm and subsequent flooding.

At least ten more inches of rain fell on September 19, with some areas receiving over 15 inches in total. Over three days of rain, the area received at least 50 inches in some locations. A number of chemical and refinery facilities were shut down in the area, including the TC Energy pipeline. The pipeline, which extends from Cushing, Oklahoma to Nederland, Texas, was restarted on Friday, September, 20. Several roadways in the area were deemed impassable due to high water, which may still be present in certain parts.

The following areas were impacted the most by the storm: 

- Chambers County: In Winnie, at least 200 homes were inundated with water and an entire hospital was evacuated. Initial estimates indicated some 800 homes were damaged in the entire county and approximately 400 people were rescued. Although it was closed during the storm, a stretch of I-10 between Beaumont and Winne has since been reopened. There are, however, reports of water on the freeway and only one lane is open.

- Harris County: In Houston, over 1,700 people were rescued, 323 vehicles were reported stranded, and a building collapsed leading to the injury of three people. In Spring, over 100 people were rescued and at least 60 people were rescued in Huffman. Hundreds of homes were inundated in the Humble and Kingwood areas.

- Jefferson County: The County received roughly 40 inches of rain over a 72-hour period. The Green Pond Gulley Levee was at risk of collapse due to deteriorating conditions exacerbated by rainfall. As a result, county officials ordered multiple evacuations as a precaution. The levee is currently in a stable condition. In Beaumont, over 250 high water rescues were performed.

- Galveston County: All Island Transit services were suspended, including fixed routes, Dial-A-Ride, and rubber wheel trolleys. 
As the post-storm process continues, authorities have stated that around 7,000 national flood insurance claims have been made. Expect residual disruptions as water, debris and other associated impacts continue to affect the region. This incident is closed.

Recovery Under Way Following Weekend Storm Packing Strong Winds and Rain Extensive damage was reported following a storm with heavy winds that swept over Malta during the weekend. Coastal areas and the northeast of the country were among the hardest-hit locations, though no injuries were initially reported. During the severe weather, authorities evacuated 14 people from Sliema and a dozen from Vittoriosa. The storm brought strong waves that damaged or destroyed many stone walls and waterfront businesses have been working to clean up debris and make any needed repairs. Damage to an undersea water main between Malta and Gozo will be repaired as seas calm, with the supply reportedly unaffected. Boats were also damaged during the storm, which packed hurricane-strength gusts in excess of 80 miles per hour while bringing nearly two inches of rain, more than half of the country s rainfall so far this month. Roadways had been partially or fully blocked in many locations due to downed trees. 
 
	Assessment: The exceptional storm was driven by two contrasting pressure systems in the region converging and driving strong winds in the highly varied barometric occurrence. Prime Minister Joseph Muscat said the storm was the worst since October 1982. The government is assessing storm damage and may seek financial assistance from the European Union, Muscat noted. Although there was not extensive damage to critical infrastructure, damage such as toppled power lines and weakened walls highlighted the need for upgrading aging infrastructure. Winds are expected to pick up again on Wednesday and Saturday, though not nearing the level of intensity as occurred last weekend. Resilience360 customers are advised to remain aware of potentially weakened structures and vegetation as storm damage assessments continue, to exercise caution in the event of further inclement conditions, and to heed the guidance of local authorities in an emergency.

- All ships and their agents are obliged to submit the IMO Declaration of Health to the Harbour Master as well as the attached ‘Coronavirus questionnaire’.
- Both documents should be signed and stamped by the Captain. Both documents need to be uploaded in the Port management system by the ship’s agent for approval of the vessel called by the Harbour Master.
- In case of a sick person on board, the vessel will not be allowed to enter the port and the patient involved will be screened by a Port Health team at anchorage.
- In case of recently arrived crew on board the ship (within the last 16 days), the Harbour Master will decide, based upon the submitted facts, whether pilot boarding and port entry are allowed.
- No disembarkation of ship’s crew is allowed during the ship’s call, including the anchorage.
- In case of needed emergency shore leave or crew change, pre-approval is needed from the Harbour Master, Immigration and Port Health. For Harbour Master approval, this request must be sent to the Port Control email address as mentioned hereunder. Approval is given by email.
- Any concerned staff interacting with the ship’s crew should follow up on the official advice from the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization on personal protection.
- Port Control should be contacted in case of any suspicious situation regarding the Coronavirus in the port area or onboard a ship so that appropriate measures can be taken in close cooperation with the Port Health team.

Hurricane Isaias to Impact Florida Coast this Weekend Before Moving up the Eastern Seaboard Hurricane Isaias is continuing to strengthen as it moves through the Bahamas towards the east Florida coast. The storm is currently a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale, with winds of at least 75 miles per hour. Strengthening is expected beginning Friday night and the storm may increase to a Category 2 hurricane. The current forecast shows Isaias skirting the east coast of Florida beginning Saturday night before moving up the East Coast. Landfall is currently forecast sometime on Monday near the South Carolina-North Carolina border. Isaias will then weaken into a tropical storm and is expected to continue moving up the coast, potentially impacting the Northeast coast. Some uncertainty in the track of the storm remains and its possible the storm makes landfall along the upper east coast of Florida late Sunday in addition to the expected landfall in the Carolinas. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) has issued a hurricane warning for portions of the central and southern Atlantic Florida coasts. A state of emergency has been issued for the entire eastern Florida coast as well as for the states of North Carolina and Virginia. 



Assessment: As of this writing, the only evacuations issued are on Ocracoke Island in North Carolina. Evacuations remain a possibility for the coast of Florida as the storm continues to move closer to land and the hurricane track evolves. Airport closures and flight delays also remain a possibility both along the eastern coast of Florida, as well as up the rest of the East Coast as the storm moves up the coastline. Portions of Florida and the Carolinas are forecast to see upwards of five inches of rain and flash flooding is possible along the entire east coast of the United States. Similarly, port closures remain a possibility but as of this writing, none have been issued. Several ports in Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia have been set to Port Condition Whiskey. This means that ports remain open to all commercial and cargo operations but commercial vessels greater than 500 gross tons should begin making plans to depart the port. The strong winds from Isaias are likely to cause widespread power outages across the eastern seaboard. Some outages may be prolonged for multiple days depending on other impacts caused by the storm. Those with interests along the U.S. East Coast are advised to continue monitoring the situation closely. The public should use extreme caution in storm conditions and heed all weather warnings and instructions from local authorities.

Preparations Ongoing, Emergency Proclamations Issued in Anticipation of Hurricane Florence On Monday, Hurricane Florence intensified into a Category 4 storm as it continued to track to the north-northwest across the Atlantic Ocean. The National Weather Service forecasts that Florence will be a major hurricane (meaning a Category 3 storm or above on the Saffir-Simpson Scale) when it makes landfall on the East Coast of the United States later this week. Tropical-storm-force winds may arrive on the East Coast sometime between Wednesday night and Thursday morning. Rainfall totals of between six and ten inches are forecast for much of North Carolina and Virginia, with an area that may expect more than ten inches arcing from eastern North Carolina to the northwest and north into central and northern Virginia. Rainfall totals may exceed current estimates if Florence lingers over the region longer than is currently expected. States of emergency have been declared preemptively by the governors of South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, and Maryland. Evacuation orders have been issued for coastal communities in South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia. Amtrak announced modified services for locations on the East Coast beginning Wednesday, September 13 due to the predicted impacts of Hurricane Florence. 
 
	Assessment: Maritime authorities are monitoring Hurricane Florence s progress and will close port operations as it is deemed necessary. Port condition Whiskey was set Monday for the Ports of South Carolina, as well as for ports in Georgia, North Carolina, Virginia, and the Maryland-National Capital Region. Shipping experts posit that Florence s impacts to shipping will depend on its exact path and intensity when it makes landfall. Disruptions to freight operations may be exacerbated by widespread flooding or damage to roads and railroads throughout the region. Locations inland have been advised to make preparations in the event that additional evacuation orders are issued, especially those areas that are low-lying or are prone to flooding. Resilience360 customers are advised to heed all local weather warnings and evacuation notices. Full coverage of Hurricane Florence s impacts can be viewed by logging onto Resilience360 s Risk Center solution.

Remuneration negotiations increase risk of temporary strikes affecting... Risks: Labour relationsSectors or assets affected: Oil and gasOn 14 August, the Oil Workers Union (Union Sindical Obrera de la Industria del Petroleo: USO) will begin collective wage negotiations with state oil company Ecopetrol. USO is demanding a 15% salary increase, with an additional 10% increase within six months, a minimum 60% increase in travel expenses and an additional 30% in other economic benefits. Colombian financial journal Portfolio estimates the demands will cost the company around USD680 million. USO represents more than 3,500 workers at Ecopetrol, around 35% of the total of the firm's direct employees. An additional 24,000 sub-contract workers are employed by the firm, according to Colombian newspaper Dinero. Other, non-financial demands include guarantees that the firm will not be privatised and an improvement in the labour rights of sub-contracted workers. In a statement on its official website on 2 August, USO said it was preparing for a general strike to defend its demands if they are not met. USO has approximately 18,000 members in the oil and gas and associated sectors, according to Ecopetrol.Significance: Although USO will support localised strikes several times a year,  it has not held a general strike since 2004, when the union went on strike over plans to partially privatise Ecopetrol, which eventually passed in 2006, allowing up to 20% of private ownership. State ownership is currently 88.49%. The issue resurfaced under the Previous Juan Manuel Santos administration. The appointment of Alberto Carrasquilla, the new Finance Minister in the current Ivan Duque administration â who once supported the full privatisation of Ecopetrol â is unlikely to assuage the union's concerns; swift agreement is very unlikely. The union is likely to deploy localised and general strikes as a negotiating tactic through August and September, to influence both remuneration demands and the government's broader policy towards the state-owned company. A general strike would be likely to last a few days, before a legal injunction forces a suspension or allows police intervention on grounds of preventing commercial disruption. Deployment of additional state security forces to Ecopetrol locations would indicate increased likelihood of impending strike action and temporary commercial disruption. UPDATE 10 - Vietnam – Recovery efforts are underway after Tropical Storm Sinlaku caused flooding. Event closed. Sources indicate that recovery efforts are underway across Vietnam after the passage of Tropical Storm Sinlaku caused flooding and landslides in multiple provinces. Over 2,800 structures were damaged, destroyed, or inundated to some capacity, while seven people were killed, and eight people were injured in storm-related incidents. The major impacts by province were as follows:

- An Giang: At least 19 homes were destroyed and two people were injured.

- Bac Lieu: Up to 87 homes were damaged.

- Ca Mau: At least 49 homes were destroyed, while 375 homes were damaged. The districts most heavily impacted were Dam Doi and Tran Van Thoi.

- Can Tho: At least 12 homes were destroyed, while 88 others were damaged in Can Tho City.

- Dak Lak: Approximately 930 homes were inundated.

- Hai Phong: Flooding was reported in Hai Phong City resulting in an unspecified number of local evacuations.

- Hoa Binh: One person was killed after being swept away by floodwaters in Tu Son commune in Kim Boi District.

- Kien Giang: At least three people died, and four others were injured. Up to 653 homes were impacted by flooding, with 175 destroyed, 446 damaged, and 32 inundated. At least 116 households were evacuated due to landslide risks in Kien Luong District.

- Lam Dong: One person was injured in Da Lat due to falling trees striking homes.

- Lao Cai: Two people were killed, and one home was damaged in a landslide in Bat Xat District.

- Nghe An: Up to 16,200 people were evacuated from low-lying areas in the province. Approximately 16 bridges were damaged by floodwaters in Quy Chau District. 

- Quang Ninh: One person was killed in Ha Long. An unspecified number of people were evacuated from low-lying areas near waterways.

- Soc Trang: Flooding and landslides damaged at least 271 buildings, particularly in the districts of My Xuyen, My Tu, Soc Trang City, and Nga Nam. One person was injured.

- Tra Vinh: Flooding and landslides damaged approximately 300 homes across the province, with 23 of them destroyed.

- Yen Bai: At least 20 homes were damaged by landslides across the province. This event is closed.

Port workers in Valparaiso threaten to resume 35-day strike On November 17, 2018 more than 500 casual workers at Chile's flagship port of Valparaiso decided to walk off the job to demand a bonus payment, more formal contracts, and improved working conditions. After a series of small demonstrations, around 50 dockworkers linked to Terminal Cerros de Valparaiso (TCVAL) finally accepted an offer put forward by the port operator and returned to work on November 30. The rest of the protesting workers, however, did not reach an agreement with Terminal Pacífico Sur (TPS), the second and most important concessionaire in Valparaiso, until December 21, 2018, which shut down shipping for over 35 days at one of Chile’s most important ports and a major commercial hub to the capital city Santiago.

The first weeks of the strike were marked by small pickets outside the port facilities and union leaders negotiating with TPS representatives. In recent weeks, however, protests in Valparaiso have turned increasingly violent and spread to other ports along the nation's Pacific coast. The conflict reached a tipping point on Monday, December 19, when strikers set barricades throughout the city and police agents repressed demonstrators with water cannons and tear gas. Protesters also got into the Dockers' Union headquarters, resulting in 20 detainees, two injured, and the destruction of much of the furniture in the building.

One day after the violent protests in Valparaiso, the striking dockworkers received support from their colleagues at the northern ports of Iquique, Antofagasta, Caldera, Ventanas, and San Antonio, the most important one in the country and close to Valparaiso.  In the southern part of the country, dockworkers at the ports of Talcahuano San Vicente and Puerto Montt also stopped their work in support of their colleagues in Valparaiso. The possibility of officially extending the strike to other ports in the country triggered alarms in sectors highly dependent on export activity, such as agriculture, food processing, and chemicals, which send products worth some USD 25 billion to foreign markets each year.

Impacts

According to the Chilean Maritime Port Organization, the strike has caused more than 50,000 containers to be diverted to other ports, with a total revenue loss of over USD 8 million. Chile’s fruit sector was particularly impacted by the strike in Valparaiso, which handles approximately 55% of Chile’s fruit exports. According to the Federation of Fruit Producers of Chile, fruit shipments from the port of Valparaiso fell 95% as a result of the port strike, going from 59,883 tons between November 16 and December 17 in 2017 to only 3,006 tons in 2018.

Meanwhile, there was a large increase in shipments at the port of San Antonio, which had already displaced Valparaiso in cargo handling and efficiency due to past port conflicts. However, not all was positive news for the Port of San Antonio, which suffered from increased congestion due to more than 20,000 additional trucks that arrived during the strike. In a normal day, according to San Antonio’s Port Authority, there are about 100 to 150 trucks that are served in an hour. However, due to the massive arrival of operators from Valparaiso, it was necessary to attend to more than 300 trucks in just one hour.

Outlook

On December 19, the dockworkers union and the port operator TPS reached a pre-agreement, which was later rejected by the dockworkers at a general assembly. The workers argued that the compensations offered by TPS are far below what they demand. Nonetheless, on December 22, workers at port of Valparaiso ended their strike, when union representatives accepted an offer from the operator, TPS, following an agreement signed between the workers and the Ministry of Labor. TPS’s offer includes a bonus of around 760,000 pesos (USD 1,100 or EUR 965), a gift card of 250,000 pesos (USD 365 or EUR 320) and a training course worth over 400,000 pesos (USD 600 or EUR 525).

On January 3, however, a group of port workers resumed demonstrations in Valparaiso, placing barricades near the Dockworkers' Union headquarters. Protesters reportedly claim that port officials have not adhered to an initial payment agreement reached two weeks ago and that as many as 22 dockworkers who participated in the December demonstrations have been denied access to the port facilities. On the same day, TPS issued a public statement confirming that the Port of Valparaiso has continued to operate normally despite the most recent demonstrations.

Lasting 35 days, the 2018 November-December strike at the Port of Valparaiso was the second longest port strike in Chile in the last 20 years and one with important implications for the fruit industry in the country. Supply chain managers should continue to monitor the situation at the Port of Valparaiso because although operations have resumed, further demonstrations are expected in the upcoming days. Moreover, it will take weeks, if not months, to clear the congestion created as a result of the service disruption in Valparaiso.

Ten Activists Arrested over Weekend Attempting to Block Dover Port During Week of Climate Actions On Saturday, ten climate activists were arrested during a protest attempting to block the Port of Dover. Four activists held a sit-in at the Eastern Docks Roundabout, with some protesters blocking the A20 near the port. Police had cordoned off part of the westbound A20 for protesters to demonstrate legally, but multiple activists also went onto the A2, where police had been diverting traffic. Several demonstrators on the A2 glued themselves to the road before being removed by authorities. The action was conducted under the Extinction Rebellion protest group. The port said it was working with Kent Police to manage  intermittent delays  from the demonstration. No instances of violence were reported during the protest.

Assessment: The demonstration on Saturday followed on the worldwide Global Climate Strike mobilization over climate change, and it is part of a week of demonstration activity around the globe to press governments to take greater action to combat climate change. While police on Saturday sought to protect the right of protesters to demonstrate legally within designated areas of roadway near the port, the protesters efforts to disrupt port and road traffic was effective in causing some disruptions and drawing attention to the demonstration, despite a relatively low number of people involved. Extinction Rebellion activists have advocated nonviolent civil disobedience to advance their causes and have previously held an array of actions effective in causing disruptions and drawing attention while requiring relatively low participation levels. Extinction Rebellion has called for two weeks of protests in central London from Monday, October 7, with the aim of having greater impact than a similar two-week London protest in April. Protests beyond the scope of conventionally authorized rallies or marches that are seeking to cause disruption are frequently not announced in advance. While such climate protests have been largely peaceful, confrontation and incidents of unrest around such events cannot be ruled out. Resilience360 customers are advised to continue monitoring associated developments for possible actions throughout this week and in October, to anticipate potential disruptions around any targeted site, and to exercise caution near all protest activity.

ReCAAP Report: Coronavirus Pandemic Causes Piracy Incidents to Double; Trend Likely to Continue On Thursday, the Regional Cooperation Agreement on Combating Piracy and Armed Robbery against Ships in Asia (ReCAAP) released a report indicating the number of piracy incidents in Asian waters nearly doubled in the first six months of 2020 compared to the same period last year. According to the ReCAAP report, there were 51 incidents between January and June—compared to 28 in 2019—with 16 reported in the Singapore Strait alone. Of the 51 piracy incidents, 49 were incidents of armed robbery against ships, while two were piracy incidents; ReCAAP defines incidents as piracy if they occur outside the jurisdiction of any state, while those occurring in territorial waters are considered armed robbery. In addition to the Singapore Strait, incidents also occurred off the coast of Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam, as well as in the South China Sea. The report attributed the increase to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and its impact on global trade.



Assessment: With the COVID-19 pandemic currently showing no signs of slowing, the associated financial hardship facing individuals impacted by the economic downturn is unlikely to ease in the near term. When coupled with the fact that commercial vessels are expected to be less secured as maritime shipping companies look to cut costs, growing poverty and unemployment could perpetuate the uptick in piracy in Asian waters in the near and medium-term future. Compared to the Horn of Africa, piracy incidents in Asia appear to be more opportunistic, often perpetrated by local fishermen merely looking to supplement their incomes by stealing scrap metal, engine parts, and communication equipment from ships and selling the pilfered items on the black market. Additionally, most piracy remains non-violent, though perpetrators have sometimes abducted crew members and held them for ransom. Therefore, mariners operating in the region should exercise a high level of vigilance at all times and ensure that appropriate security measures are in place to deter potential attackers.

Flood-Related Disruptions, Warnings to Linger Despite Improving Weather, Death Toll at Seven Flood warnings remained in effect across North Carolina on Friday after a weather system tied to Tropical Storm Eta brought more than nine inches of rainfall to parts of the state on November 11-12. The National Weather Service extended a flash flood warning for the central counties of Alamance, Chatham, Durham, Johnston, Orange, and Wake until 3:45 PM local time on November 13, while local authorities have advised that several rivers, including the Cape Fear, Haw, Neuse, and Tar, will crest between flood stage and major flood stage over the weekend. In addition to rising water levels, multiple stretches of highway and surface streets remain closed or impassable due to flooding. Affected highways of note include Interstate 95, with the northbound lanes closed near mile marker 102 in Johnston County, about 30 miles southeast of Raleigh, until at least 5:00 PM local time on Friday. Another part of I-95 was closed near Wilson but has since reopened, as have parts of Interstate 85 near Charlotte. To view up-to-date road conditions, one can consult the following webpage maintained by the North Carolina Department of Transportation: https://www.drivenc.gov/#incidents.



Five counties declared states of emergency on Thursday due to the deluge: Alexander, Burke, Catawba, Iredell, and Yadkin. Among the areas hardest hit was Alexander County, about 65 miles northwest of Charlotte, where three people died and 31 others were rescued when floodwaters from a nearby river inundated a campsite and swept away recreational vehicles and those inside. Elsewhere in Alexander County, another person died in a car accident that was attributed to a bridge washout, while a child reportedly drowned in a swollen creek in Wake County near Raleigh. At the time of this writing, the death toll from the rainfall-induced flooding stood at seven, with two others missing. Additionally, hundreds of other people were evacuated or rescued statewide, including 143 students from the Charlotte Corvian Community School, while more than 16,400 homes and businesses lost electricity. Dozens of schools delayed the start of classes or shifted to virtual learning only on Thursday due to the inclement weather, while others in the eastern part of the state closed early once the rainfall began. The weather system, a combination of tropical moisture from Eta and a cold front, also affected parts of South Carolina and Virginia. In the former, several people had to be rescued from flooded homes in York County, while southeastern Virginia saw intense rainfall and flooding as well; flood warnings were still in place on Friday.



Assessment: Conditions improved across the southeastern U.S. on Friday and drier weather is forecast throughout the region into next week, presumably facilitating recovery and clean-up efforts. Indeed, power appeared to have been restored to the vast majority of affected customers by Friday morning; however, as noted above, the threat of flooding and associated disruptions will persist in the coming days. With swollen rivers projected to crest on Saturday, water levels are unlikely to recede before Sunday, especially from low-lying roads and neighborhoods. As such, with further residential flooding and road closures almost certain over the weekend, the public should allow additional time for overland travel and exercise caution when driving, taking care not to drive around barricades or on flooded roads, particularly those covered by moving water.
