Hong Kong Protests Become More Violent and Less Predictable, Requiring a Higher Level of Caution On Friday, protests continued across Hong Kong, with violent clashes taking place in the Mong Kok area of Kowloon and the Sheung Shui area of the New Territories in the evening. Protesters left the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), which had been a flashpoint of clashes with police earlier in the week, but some reportedly regrouped at Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) and others said they were planning to carry out different actions. Friday marked the fifth consecutive day where general strikes were called from the morning, although the morning disruptions were much less severe when compared to earlier in the week. Individuals across Hong Kong also continued the daily action of walking out and occupying the streets during lunch, although there were no reports of major clashes, which took place earlier in the week as well.

The day before, Chinese President Xi Jinping issued another statement supporting Hong Kong Chief Executive Carrie Lam and called the protests a trampling of the rule of law and a blatant challenge to the one country, two systems arrangement. The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, which is a government body tasked with advising the U.S. Congress, also recommended that if Beijing intervened militarily, Hong Kong s special economic status should be suspended. The recommendation is non-binding and there were no reports that such a plan was in place.

Assessment: Protests have entered a more violent and less predictable phase since Monday, with Hong Kong seeing daily general strikes that have resulted in widespread clashes and transportation disruptions. Protesters were generally satisfied with the disruptions seen in Monday s action, which led them to call for daily strikes through Friday. The lower impact of Friday s general strike could be indicative of slowing momentum for the actions, although it could also just be a temporary pause as protesters regroup. The actions over the past week have also seen a notable shift in tactics that have made the demonstrations less predictable. Protesters have started to use  blossom everywhere  tactics, which involve impromptu gatherings in the protesters  own local neighborhoods. The objective is to divide the attention of the police force and is also in response to the government shutting down the MTR system more quickly during protests, which was used in the previous  be water  tactics that saw protesters spread from location to location by train. Flash mob tactics, which involve the locations of demonstrations being announced just an hour or two before they start, are also becoming more popular among protesters. These developments in the protest movement make demonstrations more difficult to plan for in advance and necessitate a higher level of situational awareness being observed at all times. Some areas that have seen prolonged actions by protesters, such as PolyU and CUHK, should be avoided.

The increased levels of violence over the past week, which included a protester being shot, a person being set on fire, and a man dying after being hit by a brick have raised concerns that the Chinese military could decide to intervene and restore order. However, this is an extreme step that would be an absolute last resort if it was clear that the government and police had lost control of the situation, as it would likely have severe economic and political ramifications. The Hong Kong government still has a number of other options available, such as imposing additional restrictions under the Emergency Regulations Ordinance (ERO), which could include curfews, greater powers for police, or telecommunications restrictions, that would likely be exercised before a military intervention took place. Ongoing Tensions Sustain the Risk of Clashes at Weekend Protests in Europe over Racial Justice Protest activity in recent weeks related to the Black Lives Matter movement and associated local grievances in several European countries is planned to continue through the coming weekend. Hotspots of recent protest activity with flare-ups around demonstrations, such as in London and Paris, are likely to remain so. Police in Paris have prohibited three demonstrations planned for Saturday, though gatherings are likely to occur regardless of the prohibition, raising the potential for confrontations and clashes with authorities. Some prominent German politicians have rejected alleged systemic racism among police forces, and disputes over calls for reform can further demonstration activity in the near term. As well as central squares, government buildings, and US diplomatic facilities in several European countries, protests and associated escalations have frequently occurred around controversial statues and other symbols. Sites connected with colonial history have been common targets of condemnation. 



Assessment: The bulk of demonstrators have been peaceful, though clashes with counter-protesters and police remain a risk. Authorities continue to be challenged by allowing peaceful protest while trying to deter actions that could result in unrest, as well as the ongoing difficulty of large crowds developing while COVID-19 restrictions on gatherings remain in effect. Scrutiny over policing methods and accusations of systemic racism are likely to prompt additional demonstrations by officers, and discontent among officers could results in actions such as increased sick calls, as has occurred in limited instances in the United States. Recent protests over alleged police violence and racial inequalities have also drawn attention to the lack of official data held by countries such as France and Germany, due to policies against the collection of ethnicity in demographic data, that could underscore disparities. With mobilizations continuing over the coming days, it is advised to avoid protest activity as a precaution and to anticipate potential disruption in proximity to demonstrations.

Protest Activity Easing but Continues Around Catalonia as Businesses Call for Resolution of Conflict Protests that erupted last week over the sentencing of Catalan politicians have largely scaled back following the peak of mass protests last Friday driven by the conclusion of multiday marches into Barcelona and a general strike that day. Between Monday, October 14, and Sunday, October 20, about US $3.4 million of damage occurred during unruly protests in Barcelona, the city announced on Wednesday. The protests damaged or destroyed 1,044 containers such as trash and recycling bins, burned 57 trees, and damaged nearly 7,900 feet of asphalt. Nearly 2,100 municipal police patrols drove up overtime costs, in addition to overtime for firefighters. Two cruise ships were diverted from the Port of Barcelona during the wave of protests last week. Recent protests have concentrated around government buildings, with some participants marching from university or other student locations. During a gathering of several hundred Catalan business leaders on Wednesday in Barcelona, participants called on the regional and national leadership to find solutions leading to a conclusion of the latest conflict.

Assessment: While protest activity has eased around Catalonia compared to sustained disruptive activity in the week prior, smaller demonstrations continue to be held and have the potential for similar scenes of clashes and other unruly behavior. Upcoming weekend demonstration activity is likely to draw a larger turnout than weekday protests of recent days. About 200 protesters have been detained during the spate of protests, though there has been controversy about the relatively low number of people who have been charged by local law enforcement compared to the scenes of violence and property damage, typically involving smaller groups on the sidelines or separate from larger protests. Many of those engaged in scenes of unrest have been youths, frequently seemingly aligned with anarchist-style positions as well as people supporting Catalan independence who are angry over perceived oppression and police violence. Law enforcement officers have employed equipment such as rubber bullets and baton charges in responding to some protests, and some violent groups amidst the protests have focused on confrontations with National Police deployed in Catalonia. According to the Spanish interior ministry, about 13 percent of arrested protesters were foreigners. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has resisted calls by from some right-wing politicians for Madrid to impose central control over the autonomous region, while warning that efforts to breach Spanish law will be met with  a firm and decisive response.  With protest activity expected to continue in Catalonia at least sporadically in the buildup to the national general election on November 10, it is advised to continue monitoring associated developments for potential disruptive actions and to avoid all protest activity due to the risk of further outbreaks of violence.

Hundreds Arrested Following September 20-21 Protests; Further Demonstrations Possible On Monday, media sources reported that Egyptian authorities have arrested some 400 people following a rash of anti-government protests that broke out in several cities on September 20-21. Among those detained was Mahienour El-Masry, a prominent human rights activist and lawyer who was taken into custody in Cairo late Sunday. According to reports, authorities, including plain-clothes police officers, have been stopping individuals in Cairo and checking social media content on their cell phones. Meanwhile, the internet monitoring group Netblocks says it has recorded disruptions affecting social media platforms and news sites since September 22, with some suggesting that Arabic-language editions of international media have been blocked. The moves come after a few thousand people heeded online protest calls by a self-exiled Egyptian businessman who has accused Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and the military of corruption. Demonstrations were reported in several cities and towns on September 20 and September 21, notably in Cairo, Alexandria, Giza, Damietta, Suez, Port Said, and El-Mahalla El-Kubra, with activists demanding that President Sisi step down. Clashes ensued when police attempted to disperse the gatherings with tear gas and rubber bullets. Unconfirmed reports indicated that several people were injured. In addition to skirmishes, which were most pronounced in Suez on September 21, protest-related traffic disruptions were also reported over the weekend.

Assessment: Compared to the Arab Spring protests in 2011 and the demonstrations against late Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013, the September 20-21 gatherings were smaller and appeared to be spontaneous and devoid of central leadership. Thus, while some have described the protests as the most significant challenge to Sisi s rule to date, the movement does not seem to have gained significant traction at this time. Still, given the overall rarity of protest activity in Egypt due to strict government action against unauthorized gatherings, the fact that the demonstrations materialized at all is somewhat surprising and evidence of simmering public discontent over various grievances, notably alleged government corruption, perceived authoritarianism, and bleak economic prospects. As such, the possibility of future protests cannot be ruled out in the coming days; the aforementioned exiled businessman has called for a million-man march in Egypt on Friday, September 27. Resilience360 advises customers in Egypt to avoid any public gatherings that may crop up due to the potential for violence, particularly unruly crowd behavior and aggressive crowd dispersal methods by police.

Irrespective of Panamanian government’s decision on suspension of labour contracts, strikes and protests likely from early 2021 - UPDATE 1 Panama’s Minister of Labour and Labour Development Doris Zapata on 27 November said that 96,066 labour contracts out of a total of 282,000 suspended because of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)-virus pandemic have been reactivated. Legislation suspending contracts and reducing the working day was passed in March, with the National Assembly in July extending the measure until 31 December. After this date, workers must return to their jobs under the same conditions as before the suspension; if they do not, companies will have to dismiss them, paying the corresponding severance. Business organisations such as the Federation of Commercial Associations (Federación de Cámaras de Comercio: Fedecámaras) have strongly lobbied in favour of extending the measure into 2021, as around 85% of small and medium-sized companies have said that they are likely to be forced to reopen with fewer staff, while only 8% have said that they have sufficient funding to cover workers’ severance pay. Unions oppose any extension on the grounds that affected workers have been without adequate income for the past eight months (the government funds only USD100 per month through the Panama Solidario welfare payment) and are in expectation of either the restoration of full wages or severance pay.Significance: Irrespective of the government’s decision on the future of contract suspensions, strikes and protests are likely from the first few months of 2021. In the event of an extension, unions will press for early contract reactivation, and many companies are unlikely to be able to either restore full salaries or fund severance pay. The government has stated that it is open to extending the suspension for sectors most affected by the lockdowns and is currently in discussions with business and labour sectors. If, as is likely, the National Union of Workers of Construction and Similar Industries (El Sindicato único nacional de trabajadores de la industria de la construcción y similares: SUNTRACS) rejects an agreement, there would be a high likelihood of protest roadblocks lasting for weeks at a time, causing disruption to cargo and resulting in vandalism near Colón port and Panama City. Even if an agreement regarding suspension is reached with unions, protest risks are likely to be high from early 2021. Three Attempted Acts of Piracy in Singapore Strait Overnight Sunday into Monday Amid Slight Uptick Beginning at around 11:00 PM local time on Sunday, there were three attempted acts of piracy in the Singapore Strait in a roughly two-and-a-half-hour period. Each of the situations took place off the Indonesian coast and all three involved ships in the eastbound lane of the Strait’s Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS). The first and third occurred near Nongsa Point, and the second happened off of Pulau Nongsa. Nothing was successfully stolen during any of the attempts, and there were no injuries.



Assessment: According to the Regional Cooperation Agreement on Combating Piracy and Armed Robbery Against Ships in Asia (ReCAAP), there has been a slight uptick in recent reports of piracy in the Singapore Strait, with October’s six total incidents being the highest monthly number for the year thus far. No injuries have been reported in any of the October incidents, and suspects successfully stole minor items in only one of the attacks. There have been a total of 28 piracy attempts reported in the Strait so far in 2020, compared to 31 for the entirety of 2019. Of this year’s attacks, 24 have taken place against ships traveling in the eastbound lanes of the TSS. Given the short timeframe that the Sunday night attempts occurred in, they were likely carried out by a single group of suspects. Although there were no injuries, the crew of one of the ships was unsure of whether all of the suspects had departed, and the ship was forced to divert to Batam, Indonesia, where it was searched by Indonesian naval personnel. Such diversions could cause significant disruptions for shipping even when there are no injuries and nothing is successfully stolen. As no arrests were made in any of Sunday night’s attempts, ReCAAP has warned that the same suspects may possibly try to attack additional ships. The organization advises ships in the region to take precautions and to report any incidents of piracy to the nearest government.

Several Countries Begin Lifting COVID-19 Restrictions, Despite Rising Cases and Warnings On Monday, several countries in Sub-Saharan Africa began lifting their lockdowns and other restrictions introduced to contain the spread of COVID-19. Ghana lifted its three-week restriction on movement in the Accra and Kumasi metropolitan areas on Monday, while Madagascar began progressively lifting the confinements in Antananarivo, Fianarantsoa, and Toamasina. In Madagascar, public transportation was expected to resume on Monday and schools will reopen on Wednesday. The restrictions on movement will also be lifted from 6:00 AM to 1:00 PM local time daily; however, the ban on inter-city travel will remain in place and everyone must wear face masks in public. The lockdown in South Africa also remains in effect until April 30, but authorities have stated that port operations will resume to decrease congestion. South Africa also began allowing mining companies to resume partial operations last week.



Assessment: Countries across Sub-Saharan Africa have faced increasing pressure to lift the restrictions from within the local populace, many of whom perceive the measures as affected their livelihoods. While the lifting of the measures is likely to help ease tensions somewhat, health officials have warned that lifting them too soon could lead to a rise in new cases. Much of Sub-Saharan Africa continues to experience exponential increases in cases and testing capabilities remain extremely limited, making the region particularly vulnerable to widespread, under-reported community transmission. Ghana may be one of the few exceptions, as it has ramped up testing significantly, testing over 60,000 people, and has adopted aggressive contact tracing. South Africa has also stepped up testing in recent weeks, and coupled with its lockdown, it appears to have helped stem the number of new cases per day.

UPDATE 1 - Grenade explosions in Antwerp likely indicative of drug gang rivalry, increasing security risks in Belgian port areas On 24 August 2020, unidentified perpetrators threw a hand grenade into a vacant building in Deurne, east Antwerp, with the grenade bouncing back and exploding on the street next to the house of a local drug trafficking gang leader, without causing any casualties. The attack followed two other hand grenade explosions over the weekend in east Antwerp’s Ekstelaar and Borgerhout areas, where a shooting targeting the family home of a drug gang member also took place, not leading to any casualties. Prior to the incidents, the police had seized a shipment of 500kg of cocaine at the port and detained two port employees suspected of having facilitated the trafficking of up to 800kg of cocaine, as part of a separate investigation. In 2019, Belgian authorities had seized a record 62 tonnes of cocaine in total, a 23% increase compared to 2018. The Port of Antwerp is the principal entry point for cocaine in Europe, with the substance mostly being trafficked from Brazil, Colombia and Ecuador.Significance: The increase in frequency of violent attacks between criminal gangs with the deployment of hand grenades in residential areas of Antwerp is likely indicative of intensifying rivalry between groups controlling the trafficking of cocaine into Europe through the Port of Antwerp. The escalation is likely to be linked to changes in the dynamics of drug trafficking gangs, particularly of influential drug cartels in Latin America; their revenues from extortion reduced during lockdowns introduced globally from March in response to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak. While violent attacks between gangs have so far been mostly limited to residential areas in east Antwerp, the escalation increases the likelihood of violent confrontations, including shootings and hand grenade deployment, spreading to port facilities where cargo is handled and the trafficking takes place. An increase in the frequency of checks conducted on containers by Antwerp port authorities as a response to the hand grenade attacks would probably mitigate the risk, resulting in more significant drug seizures and detention of suspected traffickers, acting as a deterrent and disrupting the illegal drug route through the port, although probably only temporarily. However, this would also lead to longer security procedures at the port, likely slowing down the handling of cargo containers. An increase in violent confrontations between criminal gangs in the city of Ghent would be an indicator of similar risks affecting the Port of Ghent, which has also been used by criminal gangs for trafficking drugs from Latin America into Europe.Risks: Criminal violence; Marine; Death and injurySectors or assets affected: All, particularly Marine cargo© 2020, IHS Markit Inc. UPDATE 1 - LNG tanker attack indicates increasing piracy and kidnap risks affecting onshore assets in Equatorial Guinea The Equatoguinean government on 17 October announced that armed pirates attacked the Marshall Islands-flagged LNG tanker Methane Princess in anchorage. The pirates reportedly boarded the vessel at the Punta Europa LNG Terminal off Malabo on Bioko Island, Equatorial Guinea’s main LNG marine pier, while it was completing a cargo operation. Reports indicate that the attackers took hostages, including an Equatoguinean and a Filipino, while another Equatoguinean citizen suffered minor injuries. The latest incident follows a growing trend of piracy and kidnap-for-ransom by criminal gangs in Equatoguinean maritime waters and the wider Gulf of Guinea, with similar piracy incidents reported close to Lomé in Togo and Takoradi in Ghana. In May, gunmen boarded the Comoros-flagged general cargo vessel Rio Mitong at anchor near Malabo and foreign and local crew members were abducted. In addition, the Equatorial Guinea-flagged ro-ro vessel Djibloho was attacked off the coast of Luba, Bioko Island, in the same month. Likewise, pirates attacked oil-supply vessel Pacific Warden near Luba in November 2019 and abducted seven out of 15 crew members. In May 2019, pirates boarded heavy-load carrier ship Blue Marlin, but later fled following a gunfight with the Spanish and Equatoguinean navies, with 10 pirates being arrested. Significance: The latest attack at the LNG terminal indicates growing operational reach and capability of these mostly Niger Delta-based assailants, while exposing security shortcomings at a strategic national asset. IHS Markit assesses that such attacks are likely to increase in frequency and would involve crew abductions and robbery of valuables other than fuel cargo. Such attacks are likely to be driven by increased investments in major energy infrastructure projects, such as the proposed development of a Gas Mega Hub. Traffic restrictions ahead of the Asian Games to impact in-land freight movement From August 18 to September 2, Indonesia will host the 18th Asian Games, a pan-Asian multi-sport event which will be held in Jakarta and Palembang. To cater to this large sporting event, authorities have increased flights at Soekarno Hatta International Airport (CGK) and Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II International Airport (PLM) which serves Jakarta and Palembang respectively. Furthermore, environmental cleanup programs, as well as traffic restrictions, have been imposed in Jakarta to curb air pollution and reduce congestion. An odd-even license plate policy on vehicles has been on a trial run since July 2 to measure the athletes’ average travel time during the events. The regulation stipulates that vehicles with license plates ending in odd numbers will only be allowed to travel in certain zones on odd-numbered dates. The same applies to plates ending with even numbers on even-numbered dates. The trial period ended on July 31 and the official implementation of the policy came into effect on August 1 again. This will last until September 2 with the hours extended from 06:00 to 21:00 (local time). The notice issued by the transportation authorities indicated that the policy also applies to cargo trucks as they fall under the category of Group III, IV and V vehicles, which includes containers and trailers.

While the games will not have a significant impact on ocean and airfreight as well as on customs clearance processes, in-land freight movement including pickup and delivery services are likely to face localized disruptions due to the scheduled operating hours of a few toll gates in Jakarta during the games. Evaluations Continue Following Severe Winter Storm That Killed 13 in Mediterranean Spain and France On Thursday, the death toll in Spain from a storm, locally referred to as Storm Gloria, rose to 13 with an additional four people missing. Mediterranean coastal areas of Spain, including Catalonia, Murcia, and Andalusia, and the Balearic Islands were hardest hit in Spain, with Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez surveying heavily impacted areas on Thursday ahead of a government emergency meeting on Friday as response measures are ongoing. The storm brought wind gusts in excess of 60 miles per hour along with heavy rain and strong waves. The majority of storm-related deaths occurred in Catalonia and Valencia. While the storm had moved from Spain, several rivers in the country s northeast burst their banks on Thursday and rice paddies in the Ebro River delta between Barcelona and Valencia were hard hit from a storm surge that extended about two miles inland. The storm also brought snow to the Pyrenees and flooding to lower-elevation areas of southern France, though no related fatalities in France are known. In France s Pyr n es-Orientales and Aude departments, as much as five months of rain has fallen within three days, prompting more than 1,500 evacuations.

Assessment: Prime Minister Sanchez said that climate change is  accentuating  storms such as Gloria, while forecasters in France noted that Gloria was the worst winter storm to strike the region since 1982. France and Spain experienced heavy flooding in October 2019, however, and both the intensity and frequency of such storms are generally believed to be hallmarks of climate change. Such storms are capable of disrupting regional transportation, damaging coastal infrastructure, and exacerbating erosion that can leave coastal areas more vulnerable to future severe weather events. In more mountainous regions, the heavy snowfall from storm systems typically heightens the risk of avalanches, and data from local officials regarding any restricted areas should be observed. While damage assessments and recovery efforts continue in both France and Spain, it is advised to continue monitoring river levels in affected areas for any further flood risk, to avoid any persisting areas of high water, including while driving, and to heed the guidance of local authorities.

Stevedore strike at Port of Santos to remain unresolved during Carnaval Sindestiva (Sindicato dos Estivadores de Santos, Sao Vicente, Guaruja e Cubatao), the largest stevedore union representing dockworkers on the Sao Paulo coast, declared the commencement of a strike at the Port of Santos on March 1 at 7:00 (local time). The strike action is the latest to involve stevedores airing grievances against the port management at Brazil’s largest seaport, and the first of 2019. 
The warning for this strike was issued on February 19, after a Superior Labor Court decision on February 11 permitted the Port of Santos to employ contractors to quantities of up to 100% of its workforce, revoking an earlier agreement from 2015 that permitted only a maximum of 50% contractor employment at the port. The strike also provides the union the opportunity to air grievances over pay and benefits. After a union meeting on February 26, the strike was confirmed on February 28, and is in progress as of this writing. 
What complicates matters is that the strike coincides with the Carnaval holiday in Brazil. Brazilian supply chains and transportation thoroughfares, like many locales which commemorate the holiday, slow down and gradually resume production after Ash Wednesday. Manufacturers traditionally give employees time off for the Carnaval period, with typical holiday duration lasting for about 1 week, starting on the preceding Friday. In extreme cases, the holiday may even extend to 21 days. Sources state that the port management and Sindestiva representatives willing to meet and negotiate during the holiday is unlikely at best.
While past incidents impacting the Port of Santos have been relatively harmless, this open-ended strike over a longer period without any negotiation in sight poses greater uncertainty. Such uncertainty without a resolution is likely to cause cargo delays and subsequent backlogs. As such, those relying on the Port of Santos as a maritime hub are advised to monitor developments. While strikes of this nature typically make provisions for the unimpeded circulation of perishable and element-sensitive goods, no such provisions have been explicitly mentioned at present.

UPDATE 1 - Australia unlikely to directly retaliate against mainland China’s targeted measures; foreign policy position also unlikely to change According to Chinese and international media reports, Chinese traders have received an informal notice from authorities that Australian products in seven categories – barley, sugar, lobster, wine, timber, coal, and copper ore and concentrate – will not be cleared in customs from 6 November. The Chinese government has denied that there are any restrictions on Australian commodities, and the implementation of the notice has yet to be confirmed. Australian exporters have nevertheless already cancelled shipments to China and Chinese traders have cancelled orders.The timing and extent of Chinese action against Australian imports give credibility to recent media reporting that this reflects Chinese government policy and not just buyers’ commercial decisions. China-Australia relations have deteriorated significantly in recent months, particularly after the Australian government called for an independent inquiry into the origins of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in April. Beginning in May, Chinese authorities imposed a series of restrictions on Australian imports, ostensibly due to alleged breaches of trade practices (resulting in tariffs on barley) or quality issues found during routine product inspections (affecting some shipments of beef, barley, lobster, and timber). On 9 October, there were reports that some Chinese ports had been told not to accept Australian coal. Although coal import quotas are not uncommon, this came days after a meeting between foreign ministers of the recently revived Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) nations, comprising Australia, India, Japan, and the United States. China has previously labelled the Quad as an “Asian NATO” (see Australia-India-Japan-US:2 October 2020: Future of Australia-India-Japan-US Quad dialogue and maritime security in the Indo-Pacific). Australian Trade Minister Simon Birmingham has accused China of taking “discriminatory action” against Australia in imposing import restrictions. China has repeatedly denied any targeting of Australia, stating that reduced imports were the result of buyers’ decisions.Given its vulnerability to wider Chinese discrimination against Australian imports, the Australian government is unlikely to retaliate. According to the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, China accounted for 32.6% (AUD153.2 billion, or USD111.1 billion) of its total goods and services exports in the financial year ending 2019. According to China’s National Bureau of Statistics, Australia in 2019 only accounted for 1.9% of mainland Chinese exports globally and 3.8% of mainland China’s exports to the Asia-Pacific and Oceania regions. This indicates that, while China has scope to extend restrictions on other Australian imports, Australia is unlikely to respond in reciprocal measures and equivalent degree. Rather, the Australian government will probably increase conciliatory advances towards China, notably through public statements on the importance of the bilateral relationship. The government is also likely to rein in backbenchers, both within the Liberal-National coalition and the Labor Party opposition, who frequently criticise China publicly. In addition, Australia will probably refrain from taking a prominent role in any further international initiatives challenging China, as it did in April when it led an international call for a COVID-19 inquiry. Repeated Chinese import restrictions are unlikely to result in Australian reversal on foreign policy issues challenged by China, however. Although Australia will avoid taking a prominent role in future international initiatives against China, its participation in the ongoing India-Japan-US Malabar naval exercise this month indicates that the Australian government is unlikely to reverse core policies that are at odds with China. This includes Australia’s commitment to the Quad grouping and its stance on issues such as Hong Kong SAR and the South China Sea. Participation in the current Malabar exercise contrasts with the last time Australia took part in 2007: China’s negative response resulted in the government of then-prime minister Kevin Rudd withdrawing from the exercises and accompanying security talks, resulting in the dissolution of the Quad. Nevertheless, given its economic vulnerability vis-à-vis China, Australia will probably seek to adjust its approach to the Quad and other regional defence activities by minimising its profile. Indicators of changing risk environmentIncreasing riskIf November and December 2020 shipments of Australian coal continue to show signs of regulatory targeting indicated by significant congestions in major ports in mainland China, this would further signal worsening bilateral relationships due to Beijing’s evident refusal to lift restrictions on Australian coal during the winter months – traditionally a period of higher power consumption and coal demand.If China imposes import restrictions or heightens regulatory barriers against Australian iron ore, this would indicate a significant worsening of bilateral relations. In 2019, 62% of China’s iron ore imports came from Australia. The economic cost of Chinese targeting of iron ore would likely be disproportionally borne in China’s infrastructure sector, which remains important in its investment-led economic recovery and relies on an inexpensive and stable supply of steel. Targeted measures against iron ore would indicate both a long-term policy shift of trade diversion from Australia to alternative markets for raw materials as well as intent to significantly damage the Australian economy, given that iron ore is Australia’s largest export to China.The passage into law of draft Australian federal legislation affecting foreign, particularly Chinese, commercial interests in Australia – likely in January 2021 (see Australia:8 June 2020: Proposed changes to Australia’s foreign investment rules likely to target Chinese investors, increasing risk of forced divestments and Australia:4 September 2020: Australia’s proposed legislation on agreements between states/territories and foreign governments indicates increased likelihood of state contract cancellation) – would be a further indicator of the trajectory of relations between Australia and China. Any amendments targeting Chinese interests more explicitly would probably result in a further deterioration of relations, increasing the likelihood of further restrictions on Australian goods and services or other targeted measures against Australian assets.Decreasing riskDirect talks between either Australian Prime Minister Scott Morrison and Chinese President Xi Jinping or their respective foreign ministers would increase the likelihood of an improvement in relations.Any delays or a government reversal on passing the draft legislation affecting Chinese interests would slightly decrease the likelihood of further Chinese restrictions on Australian products, as long as Australia avoids further high-profile diplomatic confrontations with China.© 2020, IHS Markit Inc. However, they were not successful and slowed down the pursuit. The perpetrators then fired two gunshots toward the ship’s bridge and subsequently to the ship’s accommodation. The master initiated security procedures and contacted the company security officer as well as the company’s armed escort vessel and the Nigerian Navy and carried out evasive maneuver. In addition to a man who was found dead from the storm on Sunday, overland travel complications were reported in some areas after debris damaged local roadways. Additionally, authorities responded to minor power and telecommunication outages and quickly restored service to the majority of affected customers. All schools in Salalah and eastern Dhofar governorate were slated to resume on Monday. Meanwhile, in neighboring Yemen, where Luban made landfall, 50 families were in need of evacuation on Monday after their homes were flooded in Ghaida, al-Mahra governorate. Local authorities have also ordered the temporary closure of schools and government offices amid widespread power outages across Ghaida. 
 
	Assessment: While Luban weakened to a tropical depression on Sunday, periods of heavy rainfall were forecast to continue in parts of southwestern Oman and eastern Yemen until Monday morning. As such, the possibility of further disruptions, along with possible complications to cleanup efforts, cannot be ruled out in the coming days. Resilience360 customers in Oman and Yemen should stay abreast of local weather forecasts and enact security and financial contingency plans as necessary.

Assessment: The protests were effectively a repeat of the  shop with you  actions that were held on November 10 at multiple shopping centers across Hong Kong, which also saw clashes and police using tear gas. The widespread protests on Sunday, while still smaller than many of the actions in October and early November, demonstrate that a sizable minority of protesters still have the motivation and capability to carry out disruptive protests in multiple locations at the same time. The resumption of violent protests could be tied to the Hong Kong government still refusing to make any additional concessions or substantively respond to the outcome of the local district council elections in late November, which further convinces radical protesters that they cannot rely on peaceful or political solutions to achieve their goals. While it remains unclear if Hong Kong will return to the level of violence seen in past months, the protests on Sunday represent a deterioration of the security situation when compared to the past two weeks, and there is a moderate risk of the protests escalating again in the near future. It is also concerning that police have foiled two plots involving remote-detonated explosives within a week, with the other plot involving fully functional explosives being found at a college in Wan Chai ahead of the major protest on December 8. CMA CGM Hit by Ransomware Attack; Cyberattacks on the Rise in the Logistics Industry Over the weekend of Saturday, September 27, and Sunday, September 28, the French shipping container liner company CMA CGM was targeted by a ransomware cyberattack. CMA CGM’s website and the websites of some of its subsidiaries were unavailable, except for the group’s corporate website. While initially the company stated that the issues were caused by problems with internal IT infrastructure, the situation was confirmed to be due to a cyberattack through a message on the corporate website’s homepage, as well as through a social media post by the Vice President, Joel Gentil. The Ceva Logistics subsidiary was reportedly unaffected, and the CMA CGM network remained mostly available to customers for booking and operations requests. Booking and operations services were disrupted at several Chinese offices, including Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Guangzhou. Hackers used Ragnar Locker data encryption ransomware in the attack, but external access to CMA CGM applications was purportedly interrupted when the breach was detected, preventing the malware from spreading. The full extent of the breach remains unclear. On Sunday, September 28, the hackers responsible allegedly contacted CMA CGM via email demanding to be contacted through live chat within two days to pay for a decryption key; however the price has not been disclosed. An investigation into how CMA CGM systems became infected is underway.



Assessment: CMA CGM is the world’s fourth-largest shipping container liner. The top three largest shipping liners have all been victims of cyberattacks in recent years, with Maersk in 2017, Cosco in 2018, and Mediterranean Shipping Co in 2020. The 2017 Maersk attack was reportedly collateral damage of the NotPetya cyberattack concentrated on Ukraine, and resulted in 12 days of disrupted activities and approximately $300 million in losses for the company. Logistics companies have purportedly been increasingly targeted in cyberattacks, with multimodal and automotive logistics company GEFCO suffering a breach on September 20 this year. Increased digitization of shipping and port operations are likely to contribute to increased vulnerability of the industry to cyberattacks in the future. It is advised to monitor developments associated with the investigation into the CMA CGM attack, as well as new information regarding the extent of the breach. It is also advised to monitor industry trends related to digitization and cybersecurity measures adopted by corporations in the sector as means of safeguarding internal infrastructure against future attacks.

Labour strikes: Expansion of hotel workers' strike indicates growing... On 20 September 2018, striking hotel workers from seven hotels in Chicago agreed to terms with Marriott International, ending a two-week strike. The hotel workers, organised by the UNITE HERE Local 1 union, sought wage increases, year-round health insurance coverage for workers laid-off during slower seasons, pensions, additional sick leave, and more favourable workloads. Hotel workers representing 19 additional Chicago hotels are continuing their strike, begun 7 September against various other international hotel chains operating in the city. On 17 September, UNITE HERE hotel workers in Detroit voted to authorise a strike action against Marriott, seeking similar terms to the Chicago strikers. This follows similar votes by UNITE HERE hotel workers in Boston, Hawaii, Oakland, San Diego, San Francisco, San Jose, and Seattle. Although the strikes have spread nationwide, none of them have been violent or led to damage to properties. Furthermore, none of the individual unions have called for violence.Although most hotel operators have insisted that disruptions have been minimal, there have been various media reports presenting anecdotal evidence of long check-in delays, disruptions to cleaning services, and the closure of hotel restaurants. Furthermore, two political organisations, the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the LGBTQ Health Symposium, cancelled their Chicago events in support of the strikers. Chicago's city-wide hotel strikes, the largest of their kind since 1903, represent the latest in a growing trend of work stoppages, including those involving prisoners, telecommunications workers, and teachers. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the number of major work stoppages nationwide involving 1,000 workers or more fell from approximately 350 annually in the 1970s to seven in 2017. However, per a report by Jacobin magazine, this number has more than doubled to 16 during 2018. With unemployment at 3.8%, replacing striking workers is difficult for firms. Thus, many of the strikes, as seen in the hotel example above, have been successful in accomplishing their aims and will probably provide an impetus for other employees nationwide in sectors like tourism, telecommunications, fast-food, and education. Most notably, UNITE HERE appears to have prepared well, by increasing dues prior to the action so that they could provide strike wages during the impasse. There is no precedent of notable violence during such strikes and there is no evidence to suggest this will change in the coming months. However, they are likely to last weeks or months, as shown in previous strikes with telecom firms and schools, severely disrupting business operations. Indeed, statements by the hotel union suggested that they were willing to strike months to obtain a favourable resolution to their demands. Any delay in Marriott opening negotiations with hotel workers in cities that have already authorised but not yet commenced striking would increase the likelihood of strikes in these locations, as the hotel chain has already demonstrated a willingness to address strikers' contract demands. Protests against Police Use of Force Devolve into Violent Unrest across Colombia; More Riots Likely From Wednesday night through Thursday morning, a wave of protests erupted throughout Colombia. Numerous demonstrations devolved into broader episodes of unrest, entailing arson and/or violent altercations with security forces. The catalyst behind the tumult was the death of 44-year-old law student Javier Ordoñez, which occurred the previous night.



According to Bogotá Police Commander Colonel Alexander Amaya, Tuesday evening’s incident began when Colombian National Police (PNC) officers responded to a group of intoxicated individuals who were arguing in the street in Bogotá’s Villa Luz neighborhood. Amaya claims that some members of the group became aggressive towards police. Officers placed Ordoñez under arrest, and witnesses recorded the incident on video. The recording depicts Ordoñez being pinned to the ground and tased by two police officers. Shortly thereafter, Ordoñez was pronounced dead while in police custody. The video of his arrest was widely circulated on social media the following day. 



A range of activist groups organized protests against police use of force on Wednesday, in cities including Bogotá, Medellín, Barranquilla, and Cali. As nightfall came, crowds at many demonstrations grew increasingly unruly. Rioting ensued in multiple locations, with the worst unrest being reported in Bogotá, particularly in the districts of Bosa, Engativá, Suba, and Kennedy. Demonstrators threw Molotov cocktails at police substations (CAIs) and engaged in widespread vandalism of public property. Security forces responded with tear gas and rubber bullets, and in some cases with live ammunition.



Although estimates regarding casualties have been subject to variation, local news outlets have reported that as many as eight protesters were killed nationwide. Two of the deceased demonstrators were reportedly killed by gunshots in the city of Soacha, which borders Bogotá to the southwest. Bogotá municipal authorities report that 248 protesters were wounded across the capital, including 58 individuals who sustained gunshot wounds. PNC spokesmen have indicated that 114 officers were wounded in the clashes. Media sources report that at least 30 CAIs were destroyed, 25 police motorcycles were damaged, and eight TransMilenio city buses were set on fire. Authorities report that 33 arrests were made in Bogotá, 15 in Madrid, six in Ibagué, three in Mosquera, one in Medellín, and one in Cali. 



Assessment: Defense Minister Carlos Holmes Trujillo held a press conference on Thursday morning. He condemned acts of excessive use of force among law enforcement, but also noted that various social media accounts were actively fomenting unrest and encouraging vandalism throughout the country. Bogotá Mayor Claudia López has claimed that the PNC is in need of major structural reforms, stating that “141 complaints of police abuse so far this year in Bogotá are not isolated cases.” 



Additional street manifestations have been planned across the country for Thursday night. Tensions throughout Bogotá and other large cities across Colombia will almost certainly remain elevated in the coming days and possibly weeks, and the potential for further public demonstrations will remain high. The public is advised to frequently monitor local news outlets, as impromptu bouts of protest activity could potentially crop up with little or no warning. All large crowds should be avoided as much as possible, as even demonstrations that are intended to be peaceful can rapidly escalate and devolve into violent rioting.

Risks: Labour strikes; Protests and riotsSectors or assets affected: Automotive manufacturing; Road and rail transportOn 13 November, South Korean Prime Minister Lee Nak-yeon publicly called for unionised workers to support Hyundai Motor's plan to open a new manufacturing plant in Gwangju Metropolitan City. The project envisions 12,000 new jobs, many at half the current workers' salary because of subsidies from the local authority and the plant manufacturing low-cost vehicles. Also on 13 November, GM Korea's second-largest shareholder, the Korea Development Bank, called for the firm to participate in three-way talks with its labour union about plans to spin-off its research arm, prompting fears that the manufacturing plants would close because of losses since 2014. Disagreements between the government, employers, and labour unions have persisted despite the reinvigoration of a forum for tripartite discussions and mediation: the Economic, Social and Labor Council (ESLC). South Korean President Moon Jae-in's administration remains focused on reducing unemployment (3.8% in 2018) and increasing real GDP growth (2.7%). However, it has failed to co-opt South Korea's influential unions, primarily the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) and the Federation of Korean Trade Unions (FKTU). In particular, in June, the National Assembly passed a bill revising the minimum wage act that the two umbrella unions argued would not meet demands for increased salaries, prompting them to boycott the ESLC.Significance: Strikes are likely to involve walk-outs and protests involving up to tens of thousands of people outside government buildings and firms' offices in the capital Seoul and manufacturing centres in the southeast, including Busan, Gwangju, and Ulsan. Although the risk of violence is low and would most probably take the form of union members fighting with security or harassing substitute workers, firms report KRW billions (USD millions) in annual losses because of strike action. The recent deteriorations in management-union relations indicate that strikes are now likely to last for weeks, rather than days. If the National Labor Relations Commission approves a Korea Railroad union strike scheduled around 20 November, this would indicate an increased risk of disruption to transport and operations, as with railway-workers and truckers' sympathy strikes in 2015. By contrast, if the unions, specifically the KCTU, agree to the official relaunch of the ESLC, this would be a positive indicator for negotiations to resolve pending disputes. Alleged Houthi Attack on Oil Tanker in Red Sea Highlights Threat to Maritime Security Saudi Arabian officials confirmed that a mine exploded off the coast of Shuqaiq, Saudi Arabia, and damaged a Maltese-flagged oil tanker on Wednesday, November 25. Reportedly, the MT Agrari tanker, managed by a Greek private company, was struck approximately three feet above the waterline, which caused an explosion and subsequent fire in the Red Sea, near the Shuqaiq Steam Power Plant. Following the attack, Saudi Arabia claimed to successfully intercept and destroy the explosive-laden boat that perpetrated the attack. There were no immediate reports of any hazardous contents spilling into the water and no reports of any injuries. Although the Houthi rebels have not claimed the attack on November 25, the Saudi semi-official news outlet, al Arabiya, placed blame on the Shia militant group. 



Assessment: This incident highlights the threat posed to maritime security in the Red Sea and the nearby Bab al Mandeb Strait. As the mine explosion was likely purported by the Houthis, it also stands to exacerbate rising tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Shia rebels, amid recent missile and mine attacks in the Red Sea over the past few days. Yemen’s Houthi rebels previously claimed a missile attack on a Saudi Aramco plant in Jeddah on Monday, November 23, though Aramco stated that the attack did not affect oil production. The following day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed five naval mines placed by the Houthis in the southern Red Sea. Saudi Aramco facilities are routinely targeted by Houthi rebels with ballistic missiles, drones, and mines, and such operations are likely to continue periodically in the near term. Most such attacks attempt to target ships and infrastructure along Saudi Arabia’s Western coast, though particularly bad attacks were reported last September at the Khurais and Abqaiq facilities in the country’s East. The Red Sea in particular is a critical shipping route for international energy supplies and other cargo. Damage to commercial vessels, pipelines, and production facilities in this region can affect supply chains and oil prices. More broadly, the recent attacks against Saudi interests could further increase the probability that Washington will designate the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organization, a move which would freeze all financial assets held by the Houthis in US jurisdiction and also prohibit American citizens and organizations from affiliating with the group.

Severe Storms Thursday Night Lead to at Least One Death, SOE for 11 Counties in Upstate NY On Friday, November 1, Governor Andrew Cuomo declared a state of emergency (SOE) for 11 counties in Upstate New York following widespread severe weather on Thursday night. The storms brought heavy rainfall and high winds which caused flooding and damage across the region. At least one death in Herkimer County was blamed on the flooding. An unknown number of structures across the region suffered damage in the storm, mainly from downed trees and debris caused by the high winds. Areas along the banks of Lake Erie saw significant flooding with Buffalo reporting a seven-foot rise in water levels in just several hours. Widespread power outages and numerous road closures were also reported across the region. There were no reports of widespread evacuations in relation to the storms and subsequent flooding. The state of emergency declaration included the following counties: Cayuga, Chautauqua, Dutchess, Erie, Essex, Hamilton, Herkimer, Montgomery, Oneida, Saratoga, and Warren. 

Assessment: The state of emergency declaration activated the State Emergency Operations Center to help with recovery and rebuilding efforts. In addition, at least 200 members of the state National Guard were activated to assist with cleanup and response operations. The high winds from the storm, upwards of 60 miles per hour for some areas, caused power outages to at least 241,000 utility customers at the storm's peak. As of this writing, the majority of customers have had power restored. At least 60 road closures were reported across the region, though these were mostly local roads and not major highways. An unknown number of roads suffered significant damage and will take multiple days or weeks to be repaired. Flooding has largely receded; however, rain has been forecast beginning Monday night. As of this writing, a Flood Warning remains in effect for Warren County until Wednesday, November 6 at 10:00 AM EST. Customers are advised to use caution in affected due to storm debris and the possibility of damaged roads. Heed all instructions from local authorities.

Workers had requested more personal protective equipment, hazard pay, more stringent safety measures, and more transparency on confirmed cases of the virus within the workplace. The Service Employees International Union represents more than 10,000 workers at 100 nursing homes, most in the Chicago area.

Approximately 20 workers at Columbia Farms chicken plant in West Columbia, South Carolina walked off the job on May 6 in protest of working conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic including an alleged lack of adequate pay, lack of social distancing requirements, and worker mistreatment.

Demonstrations took place across the country on May 1, also called May Day or International Worker's Day, to protest several issues. Employees of Amazon, Whole Foods, Instacart, Walmart, FedEx, Target, and Shipt embarked on a series of strikes, protests, and sick-outs to bring attention to how the companies have allegedly failed to provide basic protections against COVID-19. Additionally, residents in several states demonstrated against stay-at-home measures and other restrictions in response to COVID-19. While some protests included thousands of participants, no major disruptions were reported.

Hundreds of tech and fulfillment Amazon employees participated in a sickout on Friday, April 24, in the United States to protest alleged unsafe and unethical working conditions and Amazon’s handling of facilities with confirmed positive COVID-19 cases. The action began on Tuesday, April 21, and employees are calling for the protest to last indefinitely until Amazon meets their demands. 

Workers who deliver groceries for the Shipt app company called for a nationwide strike beginning on Tuesday, April 7. They also called for a boycott of the app on Friday, April 10. Workers are asking for additional safety precautions at no cost to workers, such as masks and gloves, hazard pay equaling an additional $5 per order, and changes to pay. It remains unclear how many of the workers are participating in the strike. The strike is intended to remain in place indefinitely until demands are met.

Instacart workers, a grocery delivery service, with the Gig Workers Collective, began a nationwide strike on Monday, March 30. Workers have stated that they will refuse to accept orders unless their demands regarding COVID-19 are met. These include additional safety precautions at no cost to workers such as hand sanitizer and disinfectant wipes, hazard pay equaling an additional $5 per order, and an extension beyond April 8 for qualification and expansion of pay for workers impacted by COVID-19 including those with known risk factors and/or those workers required to self-quarantine.

Workers at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Staten Island, NY walked off the job on Monday, March 30, and Monday, April 6, due to what they say is an inadequate job by Amazon to respond and inform employees about the ongoing COVID-19 outbreak. Employees at the Staten Island facility have alleged that there have been more COVID-19 cases there then reported and are asking the facility to be shut down for two weeks and deep cleaned. There are reports of participation at other Amazon warehouses, including in Chicago, though further plans remain unclear.

Employees at Whole Foods, a subsidiary of Amazon, held a sickout protest and refused to work on Tuesday, March 31. Similar to the Instacart strike, workers are demanding that Whole Foods provide paid leave for all workers who stay home or self-quarantine due to COVID-19, provide free COVID-19 testing for all employees, and give employees who work during the ongoing outbreak hazard pay of double the current hourly wage.

Growing Opposition Movement Calls for Demonstrations Later This Month A meeting has been called for October 2 by the 12-party alliance of opposition parties in Pakistan, known as the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM), with the aim of scheduling rallies and protests against the government of Prime Minister Imran Khan, whose Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party was voted into power in a disputed 2018 election. The meeting will be held virtually and will reportedly also appoint key officials of the PDM. The PDM’s next meeting is expected to be held on October 5. The first rally is expected on October 11 in Quetta as part of the PDM’s strategy to oust the PTI-led government. 



Assessment: The PDM reportedly intends to launch a countrywide protest movement following the Quetta rally focusing on denouncing perceived government corruption, rising inflation, unemployment, and deteriorating living conditions in the country. In addition to these grievances, the opposition movement seems to be fueled by the arrest of several senior members of Pakistan’s political elite. Indeed, on September 28, Shehbaz Sharif, the leader of the opposition Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), was arrested on corruption charges in Lahore. Protests against the arrest of Shehbaz Sharif are expected on October 3 in Lahore and October 9 in the rest of Punjab. Shehbaz Sharif was previously arrested in October 2018 in a separate corruption case while he was chief minister of the Punjab Province. His older brother, Nawaz Sharif, who previously held the position of Prime Minister three times, was forced to resign in July 2017 after the country’s Supreme Court ruled that he had lied on a parliamentary wealth declaration. He was later convicted in two corruption cases. Nawaz left the country for London on medical bail last November but has not returned since. Several other senior members of the PML-N party have been arrested during Khan’s premiership, and this strategy has been criticized by opponents as merely an avenue to strike down political resistance. Protests against Khan’s administration were also reported in November 2019, demanding his resignation, though the movement fizzled out and no major reforms were realized. The current movement has been described as being a “three-phased” plan, including countrywide public meetings, protest demonstrations and rallies in November and December, and a “decisive long march” towards Islamabad in January 2021. Heightened security is likely in Quetta in anticipation of the October 11 demonstrations including increased number of police officers, movement restrictions, and roadblocks.

Further Protests Possible After Greenpeace Ship Blocked Coal Terminal at Gdansk Port Monday On Monday night, a special unit of border guard officers boarded Greenpeace s Rainbow Warrior ship after it had anchored at the Gdansk port s coal terminal, blocking access for a ship delivering coal from Mozambique. Activists had painted  stop coal  on the side of the ship from Mozambique before the raid on the Rainbow Warrior. A group of border officers broke windows to gain entry to the ship cabins and directed a group of activists inside to lie down. The border guard said 22 activists were involved in the obstruction protest Monday, including 18 on the Rainbow Warrior and four on pontoon vessels. No injuries were reported, though activists criticized the level of force used to board and take control of the ship. The Rainbow Warrior captain and another activist were detained while the rest were released. Authorities towed the Rainbow Warrior out of the Gdansk port on Tuesday morning.

Assessment: The environmental protest did not cause long-term disruptions for port operations, though the action underscores the potential for focused protest activity to disrupt targeted operations temporarily. Greenpeace called for climate protection and a shift away from coal as an energy source for both Poland and the European Union more broadly. Activists contend that a quarter of coal burned in Poland is imported, including from countries such as Russia, the United States, Mozambique, Australia, and Colombia. While no specific further actions are known at this time, environmental activists are likely to conduct additional activities in Poland to draw attention to grievances. Resilience360 customers are advised to exercise caution near all protests and to anticipate potential operational and supply chain disruptions from any actions targeting industrial and/or logistical operations.

Protests over Alleged Police Brutality Continue across Nigeria Despite Bans and Threats from Army Over the last few days, protests have continued across Nigeria over alleged police brutality. In Lagos, demonstrators have continued to block roads, notably near the Lekki toll gate, and there were reports that unidentified thugs armed with knives, cutlasses, and guns attacked protesters in the Alausa area on Thursday. In Abuja, demonstrators marched to the gates of parliament on Thursday, defying a ban on protests. In Benin City in Edo State, demonstrators stormed the state house of assembly on Friday and clashed with armed thugs, resulting in two deaths. Additional protests have been reported in around 100 cities, including Port Harcourt, Calabar, Asaba, and Uyo. Amnesty International has reported that at least ten people have been killed in clashes with security forces since the protests began last week.



Assessment: The continuation of the protests, despite the disbandment of the controversial Special Anti Robbery Squad (SARS) police unit and promises by police to refrain from using force, suggest that demonstrators remain unswayed by the government’s concessions and may be broadening their demands. It also suggests that they likely have momentum on their side and that the protests are likely to continue over the coming days. Furthermore, the recent attacks on demonstrators risk further heightening tensions and sparking additional clashes and violence. Although the perpetrators of the attacks remain unidentified, activists claim they were carried out by thugs hired by police, further fueling allegations of repression by government forces. Conversely, the Nigerian Army issued a statement on Wednesday evening following the first attacks claiming it is prepared to “fully support” authorities in maintaining law and order. This could be perceived as a threat and suggests that the military is willing to step in if the protests continue to escalate. The public is advised to exercise an elevated level of vigilance, particularly near government buildings, police stations, and other potential protest locations, and is reminded to avoid all protest-related activities and large crowds due to the risk of violence.

Nationwide Juneteenth Actions Planned in Relation to Ongoing Use of Force Protests Widespread protest activity is expected across the United States in relation to the upcoming Juneteenth holiday on Friday, June 19. Juneteenth commemorates the full emancipation of slaves in 1865. Generally, the holiday is celebrated with parades and celebrations; however, with ongoing use-of-force protests across the United States, many activists are using the holiday for additional protests both about police use of force, as well as racial inequality. Major actions are planned in a number of cities including Tulsa, OK; Washington, DC: Los Angeles, CA; New York, NY; Seattle, WA; and Chicago, IL, among others. In addition to the expected protest activity, dockworkers with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) have planned a solidarity strike for Friday at 29 ports along the West Coast. 



Assessment: While widespread protests are likely in relation to Juneteenth, these protests are expected to have a more celebratory tone than what has occurred during use-of-force protests over the last three weeks. Many of the planned actions on Friday have been described as “block party” type events with performances like singing and dancing, rather than just protest marches. However, marches are likely to still occur and several localities, including Washington DC, have called for Juneteenth protests with intentions to block major roads and interstates. The protest action planned in Tulsa also presents a chance for escalation due to a planned rally by President Trump in the city on Saturday. The rally had been initially scheduled to be held on Friday but was pushed back following widespread public outcry. As such, the tensions at the Tulsa action are likely to be heightened and could potentially lead to clashes. Road closures are likely to be the main disruption from the Juneteenth actions; however, escalation of protest activity cannot be ruled out. The public is advised to anticipate associated disruptions and avoid protest activity due to the potential for incidental violence, such as unruly crowd behavior and/or the use of crowd control measures by law enforcement.

Protests Reported Over Illegal Housing Demolitions; Further Demonstrations Possible in Coming Weeks In recent days, protests have broken out in numerous Egyptian cities over the government demolition of “illegal” housing. In Alexandria, demonstrations reportedly took place in the Mansheya neighborhood. Protests were also reported in Port Said on September 15, and some reports indicate that other governorates, including Qalyubia and Giza witnessed similar demonstrations last month. No further specifics were provided. Additionally, on September 12, the government reduces the fines for building code violations in over 20 governorates. 



Assessment: In order to minimize illegal building on agricultural sites, state-owned land, and unlicensed multi-story buildings, Egypt enacted the Law on Reconciliation and Building Violations in 2019, which allows citizens to pay fees to the government in order to legalize their building’s status and avoid demolition. However, recent protests highlight the opposition to the law as they claim it is discriminatory towards those with limited incomes who cannot pay the fines. The reconciliation period for building violations is set to end on September 30. Following this date, an uptick in government demolitions of housing is likely. As such, sporadic demonstrations are likely to continue in the short term, though large-scale protests are less likely to manifest due to harsh crackdown on opposition in Egypt and a 2013 law severely restricting protest activity.

UPDATE 1 - Opposition parties’ losses in Jordanian election to encourage ongoing mostly peaceful protests, highly unlikely to destabilise monarchy The Islamic Action Front (IAF), the Jordanian Muslim Brotherhood’s political arm, lost five seats (down from 15) in the parliamentary elections held on 10 November 2020. Voter turnout of 30% was down from 36% in 2016, and 57% in 2013, likely due to reduced public trust in the government and in its ability to enact change due to overruling royal prerogatives. Recurring anti-austerity protests have increasingly demanded that the system of governance change to increase the power of parliament at the expense of the monarchy. Parliament’s decisions are non-binding and King Abdullah II holds executive constitutional control, and appoints the prime minister. Independent, royalist candidates from rural areas continue to be overrepresented as a result of the electoral law.Significance: The results indicate that parliament will be more supportive of government policies (see Jordan: 19 October 2020: Election unlikely to affect Jordan’s COVID-19 recovery plan, focus on reducing state spending and growing agribusiness, pharmaceuticals). This is expected to reduce delays in decision-making on contentious issues, such as likely austerity measures in the 2021 budget. Prior to the election, the government had taken several steps to curtail the opposition, including dissolving the Muslim Brotherhood and closing the Muslim Brotherhood-controlled teachers’ syndicate for two years, as well as suppressing anti-government protests through wide-scale arrests (see Jordan: 31 July 2020: Jordanian actions against dissent, including application of COVID-19 state of emergency, increase protest risk around November election). The IAF is now likely to take a less conciliatory stance toward the government, by co-operating with other opposition parties on formulating alternative fiscal and foreign policy and suggesting frameworks for political reform, notably to increase the power of the Lower House and to change the electoral law. The opposition is likely to exploit protests by unemployed people and trade unions on any austerity measures to further their goals, resulting in more frequent and protracted rallies, likely attended by several thousand people at Amman’s Fourth Circle roundabout. Any effort to increase sales or income tax or reduce subsidies or public-sector salaries would be likely to trigger protests and strikes by public sector workers. Brief Seizure of Tanker near Strait of Hormuz Reflects Persistent Risk of Maritime Incidents On Wednesday, media sources indicated that the brief seizure of a Hong Kong-flagged oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, near the Strait of Hormuz, on April 14 may have been a botched operation by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC). According to reports, armed men boarded and commandeered the Hong Kong-flagged SC Taipei, bound for Saudi Arabia, near Iran’s Ras al-Kuh coast. The ship was detained for a short time before it and its 22-member crew of Chinese nationals were released and underway under the captain’s control. A United Nations database reportedly listed the mail-forwarding address for the ship’s owners as associated with the Shanghai-based Aoxing Ship Management, which was sanctioned by the US State Department last month for “knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.” This has led to speculation that the armed men were unaware of the vessel’s affiliation, and once this was discovered, released it to avoid an entanglement with ally Beijing.



Assessment: Indeed, it is also possible that the SC Taipei had been in distress and was merely being assisted by Iran; however, it has been reported that, prior to its release, the ship was heading toward Bandar Jask, the same location where a Norwegian-owned oil tanker was taken last year after it was hit by an explosion the US blamed on an Iranian mine. Additionally, Tuesday’s episode was reportedly one of several maritime incidents near the Strait of Hormuz recently, as, according to a private shipping firm, a US-flagged container ship was approached by two boats with a raised ladder on March 27, while another tanker said it was approached by IRGC vessels on April 2. While the frequency of harassment and other provocative activities around the Strait of Hormuz has generally tapered off following a spate of such incidents last year, the tensions between the US and Iran that are widely believed to have precipitated those interactions remain escalated, leaving open the possibility that oil tankers, container ships, and other commercial vessels could be targeted as part of Tehran’s efforts to push back against Washington and its Western allies over sanctions burdening its economy. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations organization has advised vessels operating in the region to exercise vigilance and caution, and to report all suspicious incidents.

Search Continues for Two Missing Sailors from Cargo Ship that Sank Off of Vietnam The Xin Hong, a Panama-flagged cargo ship, sank near Phu Quy Island off the coast of southern Vietnam’s Binh Thuan Province on Thursday afternoon. The ship’s captain had contacted Phu Quy authorities shortly before the incident to request emergency docking permission, but the ship capsized before being able to arrive at the island. There were 11 Chinese and four Vietnamese sailors on board, of whom 11 had been rescued by Friday morning, while two others were found dead. A search for the remaining two crew members was continuing.



Assessment: The Xin Hong was transporting clay from Malaysia to Hong Kong. The accident occurred in rough seas during inclement weather that is believed to have shifted cargo, which caused the ship to list to the side before capsizing. Disruptions to shipping activities are possible in the area while search and rescue operations are carried out for the two outstanding sailors, and there is also the potential for transportation problems arising from loose shipping containers fallen from the ship.

UPDATE - Cuba: Significant disruption reported as clean-up operations commence following overnight tornado in Havana Significant disruption has been reported since the passing of a deadly tornado overnight in Havana. Known casualty figures remain at three fatalities and 172 injuries. Clean-up operations are understood to be ongoing on Monday, 28 January, with various infrastructural damages reported. Power outages remain. Flooding additionally occurred in areas including Santos Suárez, Luyanó, Via Blanca, Regla and Chibás, as well as Pinar del Río, Artemisa and Mayabeque provinces. Traffic restrictions severely disrupt container movements in Mumbai On August 21, local sources reported that traffic restrictions imposed by the police department in Thane city, a suburb of Mumbai, have severely disrupted export-import container movement at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) since August 9. The restrictions have been imposed to allow repair works of the Mumbra-Kausa bypass road and a flyover along the road. Container movement to the following terminals are impacted: Gateway Terminals India, Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal (NSICT) and Nhava Sheva (India) Gateway Terminal (NSIGT). The traffic restriction for a few hours on an arterial road linking India’s busiest container port has roiled evacuation of import containers from the port to the container freight stations (CFS) and movement of export boxes to the port, resulting in congestion. As a result, police has stopped traffic movements from and to all terminals from 05:00 to 11:00 and from 17:00 to 23:00 on a daily basis from August 16 for one month, further exacerbating the situation. Trucks will reportedly be stopped at the PUB - Y junction. This week, tractor trailers carrying containers have been stuck on the road for 8-10 hours and inventory has piled up at the terminals.

UPDATE 1 - City Council approves declaration of support for Nobel Plastiques workers Updated media sources indicate on September 25 that the board of Cornellà de Llobregat City Council (Barcelona) has approved a declaration of support for the workers of Nobel Plastiques Ibérica de Sant Joan Despí, who went strike after the company announced the closure of the plant. The decision to close the plant will affect 200 workers. Nobel Plastiques Ibérica is a subsidiary of the Turkish group Orhan Holding and is dedicated to manufacturing automotive parts. Nobel Plastiques develops and manufactures plastic and rubber automotive products. The Company creates lines and tubes for the transfer of fluids and specialty plastic shaping tools. The strike has forced Renault to suspend its afternoon shifts earlier this month at its Villamuriel de Cerrato factory and has also affected the Valladolid Assembly plant. Renault officials said that if the Nobel strike were to be prolonged, it will order parts from other suppliers to meet demand.
